- Self-accountability: "It's all on you. The self part is what's big." He says he had no trainer, no nutritionist and nobody waking him at 3am. Self-discipline is everything and "we count on people too much to get us through."
- Authenticity and motivation vs drive: he says motivation "comes and goes as how you feel"; the goal is to move from motivated to driven to obsessed. He says people can read through someone who preaches but doesn't live it.
- Truth as fuel: if someone calls you fat or dumb, "you might be." Take it, and use it as fuel. He credits his past suffering with making him appreciate happiness more: "Don't misunderstand the passion... happiest person in the world. But I'm not done."

chunks.heading: The pull-up record and doing what he hates
chunks.text:
- He set the world record for pull-ups in 24 hours: 4,030 in 17 hours (he weighed about 207 lb, sets of five, with witnesses for Guinness). He did about 67,000 pull-ups in 9 months to prepare.
- He failed twice first: about 2,588 in September in front of millions of viewers, then again 2 months later, then succeeded on January 19. His hands took third-degree burns and he tore his forearm.
- At the finish he felt nothing but relief that he could stop: "I ain't got to do more [ __ ] pull-ups anymore."
- He doesn't enjoy running or pull-ups. He says he does them because he doesn't like them: "That's the only way to callous your brain." He says people who assume he loves it are putting a label on him: "Anybody's capable of doing [ __ ] like this."
- Visualization detail: he listened to the Rocky song (2 minutes 13 seconds) on loop for 17 hours during the pull-up attempt.

chunks.heading: Current life, habits, and mission
chunks.text:
- Routine at 43: he runs every morning, lifts, and stretches at night. He stays off social media and phones to "silence the world," because he believes phones and cameras pull you away from your own mind.
- He plans to break a record crossing from Death Valley to the top of Mount Whitney as fast as possible.
- Business and brand: he runs Goggins LLC, does motivational speaking, and is investing his own money in the brand rather than chasing income. He lives on a small military retirement and calls himself a minimalist (backpack, pull-up bar, running shoes, Subway sandwich).
- He says he wants to grow it slowly and authentically, because he refuses to "mass produce" quotes or say things he doesn't live.
- His stated reason for sharing: he calls it his duty, "I'm a tool," to tell weak, scared people like his past self the unfiltered truth. He explains his heavy profanity as his refusal to water down how violent the struggle was.
- Where to find him: @davidgoggins on social media.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In this Rich Roll conversation about Can't Hurt Me, Goggins explains how he rebuilt himself from an abusive childhood, illiteracy and 300 pounds into a Navy SEAL and ultra-runner. He covers radical honesty and vulnerability, visualizing the finish and the hard moments, resetting your "new norm," taking souls, the cookie jar, journaling, and why suffering strips away artificial layers.

chunks.heading: The accountability mirror and owning your own story
chunks.text:
- David's central premise is that "the most important conversation is the one you have with yourself." You wake up with it, walk around with it, go to bed with it, and eventually act on it, so the internal dialogue has to change before anything else does.
- The accountability mirror started when he was a junior in high school. His mom found his report cards after he had been hiding that he was flunking most of his classes, and she told him he was done.
- It was not a fix. It was a starting point for holding himself accountable.
- Being honest with himself meant admitting character flaws: "I've lied about this, I've cheated here, I'm insecure here."
- He had to stop building on a "fucked-up foundation" and get down to "the actual mineral soil of who I was naturally" before real growth started.
- Reframing vulnerability: he calls being vulnerable the one thing that made him who he is. Breaking himself down to rock bottom and telling people who he is became strength, not softness.
- He self-published so he could own 100% of his story. He did not want anyone telling him what he could or could not say about what he suffered.
- Many people are going through the same things and "just hide better than you did." Stop hiding and people can understand you.
- He is not here to judge. He says the problem is that people die with untapped potential because they think someone else is better than them.

chunks.heading: Journaling, the cookie jar, and the schedule
chunks.text:
- Journaling: for several years he has kept small green military notebooks and records his day, then goes back and studies it.
  - It works as an accountability journal for physical, mental, and eating habits. He calls himself "a lab rat" who studies himself.
  - When he feels off or overtrained, he checks last week's entries to find where he messed up, such as sleep or time.
  - The journal has to be honest. "You cannot put bullshit in there."
- External accountability: circles of people matter at first. If you are a drunk, get away from the people who keep you drinking. Build a nucleus of people who say it's not okay to sleep in today.
  - The goal is to reach the point where you hold yourself accountable and those people fade, because "they're not always gonna be there to hold your hand."
- The cookie jar: in hard times even the hardest person forgets how badass they are.
  - He reaches into a mental jar of past wins: surviving three Hell Weeks, Ranger School, a brutal childhood, and seeing people die.
  - It reminds you that you can get through the current hard moment, because bad times consume the mind and make you forget who you are.
- The schedule: his answer to "I don't have time" is that you have not prioritized yourself.
  - Write down everything you do in one day. He says people discover they waste hours on phones, Instagram, texting and tweeting.
  - Everyone can find an hour a day. After that it comes down to willingness.
- His own schedule: his fiancée Jennifer builds it backward from fixed events. A 7 a.m. event an hour away means he is up by 4 a.m. to run, and sometimes 1:30 a.m. He prefers 7 to 8 hours of sleep but says the schedule sometimes allows three.

chunks.heading: Visualization, a new norm, and staying present
chunks.text:
- Visualization: he says he can "see the end before the beginning even begins."
  - Before BUD/S he pictured himself walking across the stage to get his graduation certificate at 191 pounds, and replayed that feeling many times a day.
  - That imagined feeling made the suffering feel worth it. For a race he rehearses how he will feel at mile 50, so when it arrives "it's no surprise."
- Compartmentalizing: for the ASVAB he first needed a 50 on mechanical comprehension (his earlier score was 44). He then had to lose 106 pounds in a limited time.
  - He handled one task at a time. The weight did not matter unless he first passed the test.
  - He got exactly a 50. He describes it as putting everything he had on one bet, like pushing his last chips onto the table.
- Focus: he stays fully present with whoever or whatever is in front of him. He says multitasking means half-assing everything, and that being focused on the task at hand is a huge advantage today.
- Set a new norm: while repeating the first phase of BUD/S, he reset his mindset. "Your new norm is you wake up at 4 o'clock and you suffer."
  - Once suffering is the baseline, the hard thing stops feeling hard.
  - He applies the same logic to running: a two hundred mile run becomes the new norm.
- Day one, week one: he lives by that mentality, but says he made the mistake of trying to put it on people who did not want it.

chunks.heading: Taking souls and finding energy when there is none
chunks.text:
- Taking souls means finding the tactical advantage in a hard situation, not hurting the person you are up against.
- David's reasoning: everyone has demons, and "the most alpha males are very fragile." Ego is serious. He grew up with a fragile ego and did a "live autopsy" on himself, so he figured it could be used in the instructors' heads.
- The Hell Week example: the boat crew was freezing, shaking, and jackhammering with cold. Instructors enjoyed watching them suffer.
  - He asked himself what he would hate to see if he were an instructor: students acting like it was just another day on the beach.
  - He told his boat crew (Chris Kyle was on it) they were going to "take some souls." They threw the boat overhead and caught it, and yelled while doing it.
  - He says the instructors' faces looked "numb," and the crew went on to win nearly every race.
- The takeaway: it is about finding energy and strength when you have none.
  - Energy does not have to come from outside, like a TV, podcast, or music. A lot of life is quiet, and those are the moments you want to run and hide.
  - You have to make up games and tricks to reach the next evolution, to stay in the fight until the second wind arrives.
- A related example: on Wednesday night of Hell Week, instructor SBG sent him alone to swim out through the surf zone at night with no swim buddy. He took it as his chance to show him and did it. SBG later told him he knew David would treat it as a challenge.

chunks.heading: Motivation, obsession, and why anger is not fuel
chunks.text:
- Anger can start you off, but it is not sustainable. David says anger was never his fuel.
  - It got him to look at things and say he wanted to be somebody, and it built big ego chips.
  - When he was suffering and at wit's end in cold water, the anger was gone. He was thinking only about getting out of there.
- Motivation is only a spark, like the sparks that start California wildfires. A bit of water puts it out.
  - Kindling grows only if you keep feeding it. He wants it to become a big log that burns long.
  - Motivation has to become drive, passion, and obsession for what you want to become. He calls that "an inferno."
- Obsession is self-generated, cultivated deep inside. Someone else cannot fuel you into it.
  - He calls "obsessed" a compliment, though it can ruin your life.
  - To be great at something you may be misunderstood by everybody. "You've arrived when you are misunderstood to the point where people think you're psycho."
- On balance: balance matters for many people, but going to the edge takes every second of your life.
- On January 1 resolutions: he says the kindling usually burns out within 10 to 12 days. He stopped giving people workout programs because they want a program or a watch instead of getting the shoes and running.
  - His challenge is to see how far you can take it past 12 days. "There is no hack."

chunks.heading: Staying uncomfortable, avoiding complacency, and judging yourself only against yourself
chunks.text:
- Sacrifice and discomfort: the culture pushes the idea that happiness comes from luxury, comfort, and ease. David says self-knowledge, self-esteem, and peace come through sacrifice and getting uncomfortable.
  - He says people want results in two days, and there are real plateaus, so patience matters.
  - Getting up when it's snowing and going to the gym is "miserable," and that is the point.
- Judging yourself: the biggest stumbling block is the "woe is me" mentality. People look left and right and judge themselves against others.
  - "We are judging ourselves against too many people." You have to race against yourself. He says the race is "David Goggins and David Goggins alone."
- Suffering strips away layers. In misery your internal dialogue is unfiltered and has no lies. That is who you really are.
  - Forcing yourself to stay in it builds calluses on your mind, and that is where growth happens.
  - His first hundred-mile race (Badwater) came with zero training. He says he lived five years in 19 hours of highs and lows. He did not quit, and it broke him down to nothing.
- Complacency: becoming civilized is, in his words, "the worst thing that can happen to a person." You get to the point where you believe you have arrived.
  - At 43 he cannot go as hard as at 20, but there is a new bar you must always set.
  - He keeps that bar high by returning to where he came from. He compares it to going back to the fundamentals in basketball.
  - He pays rent mentally on the $7-a-month place where he grew up.
- Going back to scratch: he is working as a wildland firefighter, which he says means being a nobody again on a fire line. He values being nobody and likens it to Ranger School, where titles are removed.
- He distrusts people who talk about what they used to do. He wants to know what you are doing today. "I hear so much talk, I don't hear a lot of work."

chunks.heading: Peace, purpose, and the fear of failing the mission
chunks.text:
- Peace: he says he never found peace until he got really sick.
  - Peace comes from clarity, and there is no clarity when there is noise.
  - He found it by looking back at the dungeon he came from. "The greater the suffering, the greater the peace I've found."
- Taking a vantage point: inside a grinding schedule you need a point (he says 12 o'clock) to reset and survey what you have accomplished.
  - He and his fiancée now stop to appreciate what they have done. They were so busy grinding they lost sight of it.
  - If you do not step back, you never apply what you learned. He says he would have handled the second platoon differently if he had.
- Overtraining: after two heart surgeries and a return to ultras, he overtrained and his thyroid and endocrine system broke down. It lasted about five years, starting around 2013.
  - He calls it one of his hardest and most eye-opening times. He could not run or train, so he went to school and became a medic.
  - He was always pursuing his "hundred percent," whatever form it took.
- His father: he found peace by going back to where it started and forgiving a man who hated himself. His father never said sorry, and they last spoke when David was 22. He died four or five years before this interview.
- Being nonjudgmental: it had to be learned the hard way. He used to want to fit in and "swore" he wanted people to like him, which he says makes you lose yourself.
  - Now: "take a number and get in line."
- His faith: he believes in God and describes a voice in his head since he was a young kid that guided him.
  - He sees his past as the perfect training ground, with every domino lined up.
- His biggest fear: getting to heaven and being shown a chart of who he was supposed to be, and having under-achieved against it.
  - He wants whatever force knows what he is capable of to say it had "no idea he even had this in him."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins explains how he built a "warrior mentality" out of an abusive, racist childhood by putting himself through self-designed crucibles (Hell Week, Badwater, 100-milers). He covers the accountability mirror, the cookie jar, embracing suffering, callousing the brain, reframing failure, and why excuses and endless "how" questions keep people stuck.

chunks.heading: Callousing the mind: how David builds a "warrior mentality"
chunks.text:
- David says he was born with no mental toughness: abusive father, raised in a small Indiana town near Klan headquarters, called the n-word daily, learning disabilities, "zero" self-esteem, and a high school graduation where he cheated on tests and homework.
- A teen meeting with an Air Force special operator gave him a goal ("my real-life Rambo"). He saw himself as "the weakest human being on the planet" and wanted to become "the hardest man God ever created."
- He flipped his mindset: instead of "why me," he treated the bad hand as "the platform" for who he wanted to be.
- He deliberately designed crucibles (SEAL training, ultra races) to build a warrior mentality: "I was building that callous mind."
- He says he also callouses his brain the way pull-ups callous hands: by moving through hell, ignoring negativity, and running "to the fight" instead of from it. That is how he handled PTSD.
- He created "Goggins" as a persona. "David Goggins was a weak kid so I created Goggins." This was conscious and internal: "I don't care about money, awards, medals." The aim was to be proud of himself.

chunks.heading: The accountability mirror
chunks.text:
- He started shaving his head and face at 16 and used the time looking at his reflection to tell himself the truth: he was dumb, a cheater, a liar, insecure.
- Core idea: "If you suck, you suck. If you tell yourself you suck, that is when you become great." He rejects friends and circles that keep giving positive feedback to someone who is dumb or fat.
- It is a daily practice he still does. If he tells a white lie, he confronts himself in the mirror next morning, like a daily inventory.
- He says to handle insecurities and jealousies before chasing a goal, because they surface when you are suffering in the crucible. "The ego will kill you every time."
- He ties staying power to purpose: leave the ego at the door and know why you are doing it.
- He is critical of participation trophies and "everyone is great" culture. Without them he says he would not have become who he is.

chunks.heading: The cookie jar and the first 100-mile race
chunks.text:
- Origin: he called the Bad Water race director on a Wednesday in November 2005 and was told to qualify with 100 miles in 24 hours. Three days later he ran the San Diego One Day, a 24-hour, one-mile-track race, with zero training at roughly 250+ lb.
- Setup: a blue lawn chair, Mike and Ike candy, Ritz crackers, and his then-wife crewing.
- Around mile 50 he broke bones in his feet (stress fractures, shin splints). At mile 70 he sat down, and when he tried to get up he urinated blood and soiled himself. He says it was the worst thing he has endured, including SEAL training.
- The cookie jar: every time he failed and then succeeded, he put a "cookie" in the jar. When suffering makes you forget how great you are, he recalls where he came from with a calm mind and then solves the problem: salt, electrolytes, food, hydration, and fixing blood pressure first so he could stand.
- Pace: he was walking a 37-minute mile. At mile 81 his wife said he would not make the time, and he ran the last 19 miles. He finished 100 miles in 18 hours 56 minutes.
- He says this showed how far short human beings stop when they feel pain.

chunks.heading: Embracing suffering and the "what if" mindset
chunks.text:
- At mile 70 he says he had to "go dark" into a "barbaric, garanimal mindset" and make the suffering work for him: "I embraced the suffering."
- He talked to himself with a "what if": what if I get through this while this messed up? He pictured finishing and the feeling afterward, which sparked his endorphins.
- He denies being a masochist: "I'm not a crazy guy. I'm a guy that wanted to see who the best me was." His journey was to find his limits and not settle for stopping at 70.
- Moments of extreme difficulty reveal character: "It's all about that moment and that decision you have to make when everything else is stripped away."
- Hard evidence of the breadth: he did the 100-mile Hurt 100 about two months later with the feet still broken, finished Jan 17, and then ran Badwater (fifth place the first year, third the second) with compression tape on his shins, training only 30 to 40 miles a week on feet that were broken.
- Cross-training for that: heavy time on the sauna, elliptical, and rucksack.
- In 2007 he says he ran many 100-milers in consecutive weeks (Western States, Leadville, Angeles Crest, Bear, and others) and treated each one like "another workout."

chunks.heading: Reframing failure and rejecting "freak" excuses
chunks.text:
- Failure to David is just "more information on how to succeed." He fails, goes back to the drawing board, and tries again. You must be willing to fail 100 times to succeed once.
- Example: he failed a pull-up record attempt, took two months off, failed again, then set the record (4,025 pull-ups in 24 hours) in January. He did 67,000 pull-ups in nine months to train.
- He says people call him a genetic freak, but he has sickle cell and a hole in his heart, a low VO2 max and bad hematocrit, and says he operates on a fraction of capacity. Everything he did was "miserable" and he was destroyed at mile 50 of every 100-miler.
- He refuses to let people excuse themselves by putting him in a category. "You watered down my message by putting me in a category."
- 2013 Badwater: he walked 105 miles, spent about seven hours in the vehicle, and treated it as resetting the goal rather than quitting.
- Fun detail: his first Ultraman (borrowed bike, three weeks of bike training) ended with a flat and no clips, and he rode 75 miles on pedals in running shoes and missed first by about 10 minutes.

chunks.heading: Stop asking questions: want it and start
chunks.text:
- David says people stall by asking endless "how" questions (what watch, what plan) and by saying "I wish I could." "Stop asking these questions... get an idea, start walking, and figure this out as you go."
- His examples: he qualified for Badwater in days and ran it, lost over 100 pounds in about 60 days to get into SEAL training (he says 105), and became a Ranger at 41.
- Time excuses: while a full-time SEAL he woke at 3 a.m., ran, then rode his bike to work. "If you want it, you will find time in your life to do it. If you don't want it, you will continue to give excuses."
- The passion that people read as anger is, he says, because he knows it can be done.
- Many people say they will do something "one day" and he says most do not want anything badly enough.

chunks.heading: Motivation vs. purpose, and changing how you think
chunks.text:
- He says motivation is "crap" compared with being driven. The windchill example: a motivated person goes back inside; a driven person goes back in to get a new hat and runs anyway.
- Purpose requires quiet: tune out social media and others' noise and listen to your internal voice. Many people never listen to what they want.
- He says people change their car, underwear, spouse, or diet but rarely "the way they think," which keeps them stuck.
- Key message: "If you want to be better, you have to change your perceived limitations and take the barriers down." He is "working on how most people think" and tailors his message since people respond to different things.
- He says what you do for fulfillment: find "the truth of who you are" and take the hard journey rather than the "journey of least resistance."

chunks.heading: Keeping the edge, stretching, and health lessons
chunks.text:
- Even when successful, he says "the worst thing that can happen to a man is he becomes civilized." He keeps his mind sharp "like a sword" and keeps "the refrigerator empty" so he always keeps an edge.
- He values a simple life (backpack, Subway sandwiches, push-ups, football in a hole-in-the-wall) and sees luxury as not for him after staying with the Itzlers.
- Health price: his adrenals are shot, and he has a heart defect, sickle cell, and spinal issues. He says he knew what he was doing to himself and sees it as worth it.
- Stretching routine: he stretched 8 to 12 hours a day at the worst point, then 6, then about 2, and has not missed a day in three years. He focuses on the psoas, hip flexors, and abductors, holding stretches 30 to 40 minutes, and says it fixed back pain and a bump at the base of his skull.
- Results he claims: his Rocket-style 41-mile race pace improved from 8:30 to 8:40 training pace to about 7:15 to 7:30, and he cut his time on a course from 5:30-something to 4:50. His advice is to do your own research and be your own guinea pig.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins explains why mental toughness is a perishable skill that must be rebuilt daily, how he controls the "one second decision" to quit, and why confidence is built from earned proof, not affirmations. He also covers capping success, trained humility, and armoring the mind each morning.

chunks.heading: Laziness is beaten by raising your standard, not by waiting for motivation
chunks.text:
- David argues motivation is not a permanent fix. "You have to learn to perform without motivation. You have to learn to perform without purpose."
- Motivation is "kindling to the fire"; all it takes is a spark to burn a forest, but you must be your best self "when you're least motivated."
- Most people fail because they think they need motivation to work out or study. If they don't have it, they don't do it.
- His test for laziness: if you wake up and don't want to do the thing, you don't care enough about yourself. Research why you aren't doing it for yourself.
- Hard days stack up (cold, dark, warm couch, argument last night, hungover). He says that is exactly how you level up, and he is happy that so many people with ability refuse to get off the couch, because that gives him the advantage.
- "It's so easy to be great nowadays because most people are weak." Most won't go the extra mile because it is miserable and lonely, and he thrives in that loneliness.
- Performance without a purpose: even with no race, class or goal on the docket, keep performing at the highest level, because when the thing finally arrives you won't be ready unless you were already training.
- "You are always the purpose." The main purpose in life is to better oneself, and that is the only purpose he needs.

chunks.heading: The one second decision
chunks.text:
- Pain pushes the brain into fight or flight, and it is hard to process information rationally while in pain.
- He uses SEAL Hell Week (about 130 hours) as the example. It starts as a pep rally with guns and grenade simulators, then goes quiet and marches you into the surf for surf torture. Your mind jumps from hour 2 to hour 130 and you forget every reason you wanted to be there.
- In that moment, all you want is warmth, food, and your girl holding you. That is the one second where people lose; lose it once and you lose the whole thing.
- His tactic: physically stay in the water (getting out is quitting), but mentally go stand on the beach with the instructors in their Parkas with coffee. Now "warm" mentally, think logically.
- Then ask: where are you going to end up if you quit? What will you say to yourself? He projects forward to the long-term shame and regret versus the pride of finishing.
- He says people who quit Ranger school, SEAL training or Air Force training still call him decades later, unable to enjoy their lives because they are thinking about what they could have been.
- "I don't look at failure anymore as failure. I look at it as my first, second and third attempt."
- Daily question: "Can I take one more step?" Usually the answer is yes. Not taking it when you can is real quitting, and "that's on me and I gotta live with that."

chunks.heading: Moab 240: re-qualify mental toughness and make the new level your norm
chunks.text:
- Mental toughness is "a perishable skill." Going through training once does not last forever. He says you must recall it and re-qualify "every day, not once a year."
- Before Moab he had gone about 6 years without a 100-mile race, had heart surgeries and small injuries, and felt he had become "part-time Savage." He decided to push to the next level with the 240-mile race.
- First attempt: he got lost, got sick (pulmonary edema), slept about 12 hours, then got back in the race. A doctor told him that leaving the course meant he couldn't come back, so he left it. The race was already a DNF for him.
- Lying in bed, he heard a voice, "You're not done yet." He woke his wife Jennifer and two crew members, had her drop him at the spot where he left, and finished the last roughly 40 miles. He finished next to a telephone pole, not at the official line, for roughly 250 to 255 miles total. He says it was one of the best races of his life.
- He came back and did it better. His point: pushing a limit makes it your new norm. A 240-mile race became as easy as running 50 once he figured it out.
- At mile 201 on the second attempt his rear was raw like hamburger meat from chafing, and Jennifer applied the cream.

chunks.heading: Gaining knowledge through staying humble, capping success, and the mental lab
chunks.text:
- Success can make you soft. His fix is to "cap success": stop hearing yourself talk, get off podcasts and social media, and "get back to the mental lab," because that is where his knowledge comes from.
- He says he does few podcasts, and after finishing a 10-day book push he said he probably wouldn't do another for a very long time. He goes back to firefighting to find the next level.
- He keeps growing at $12 to $15 an hour as a smoke jumper (Wildland firefighting in British Columbia, jumping into spots vehicles can't reach, with gear dropped separately, up to 7 days on the longest job). He turned down millions to do it, and says the growth is in the freezing, questioning-yourself moments.
- Trained humility: stay hungry but stay humble within the hunger. He cites William Crawford, a Medal of Honor winner who worked as a janitor at the Air Force Academy, cleaned for young cadets, and treated himself as no better than anyone.
- His message must not be cookie cutter. It needs to be broad enough that all 25 people in a room get something, which requires constant reinvention.
- "Take what I say with a grain of salt." His mission is different from yours.
- On the SEAL tear gas story and Elon Musk demanding hard work at Twitter: he doesn't judge. Some people want that environment, and society needs people willing to do those jobs. If you don't understand someone like him, it probably means he is in an area of life you're not in.

chunks.heading: Organizing the mind: the garage, meditation, and the daily routine
chunks.text:
- Discipline and motivation don't work if the brain is cluttered. He compares the mind to a cluttered garage where you can't find your dumbbells. You need it organized (he calls it "mental zones") so discipline and consistency each have a shelf.
- Life stressors (kids, wife, job) all stuffed in your head are why people fall off the wagon.
- He meditates and stretches about two hours every night (one 4-hour block combined with stretching, per the conversation) to "reorganize the garage."
- Morning routine:
  - Up about 5 to 5:30.
  - Fasted run every morning, minimum 12 miles, in heart rate zone 2 at roughly 8:15 to 8:30 pace, about 1.5 to 2 hours. He is retraining from scratch after his leg injury.
  - Run is his "cup of coffee" because it's what he hates most. He calls it armoring: "armor plate my mind and body like a person going to war" before opening his phone.
  - Eats something small, then gym 45 minutes to 1.5 hours.
  - Stationary bike 3 to 4 days a week, plus stretching and meditation at night.
  - Sleeps 7 to 8 hours.
- This has been his routine for seven years, and he says the only reason he can fit it all is that he caps success.
- He doesn't carry his phone; it is the biggest distraction and he wants to be present.

chunks.heading: Building real confidence through proof, not affirmations
chunks.text:
- Skeptical of pounding your chest and shouting affirmations in the mirror. What works for him is an everyday resume of real accomplishments: "the real calluses on my mind, the real calluses on my hands."
- He agrees with the idea of a "stack of undeniable proof": three Hell Weeks, Ranger school, Delta selection.
- "Built belief" versus "after school special belief." Confidence must come from the work you put in, not just being told to believe.
- Don't make dreams your master: people talk about being a Navy SEAL or astronaut and get a dopamine kick from the talking, then the 4 a.m. alarm goes off and they skip it. You become master of the dream when you do the laundry list of tasks (he lost 106 pounds in under three months to try to become a SEAL).
- Limited horizons: coming from a small Indiana town (about 8,000 people), his mind could only picture what he had seen. He credits being able to dream beyond those four walls.
- He found his first 100-mile race (San Diego 24-hour track, he was a bodybuilder doing 20 minutes of cardio a week) by Googling the world's toughest events to raise money for the Special Operations Warrior Foundation. He says the roughly 31 mile final stretch was the worst pain of his life, yet it showed him "what is possible" and that he had been "underachieving my entire life." He cautions it is a dangerous place (near rhabdo).

chunks.heading: Using haters, bullies and the past as fuel
chunks.text:
- Hater mixtape: he reads comments, deletes and blocks the nasty ones from his page, takes a screenshot, and archives them. He turns them into audio and plays them on a loop while running as fuel. His reasoning is that haters are usually underachievers, so he'll keep succeeding to make them question themselves.
- Doesn't take the hate personally. "You'll never meet a hater doing better than you." He studies the haters, since he was once that negative person himself, and feels pity.
- Example: a former SEAL Team Six guy attacked and lied about him; he was ready to sue but after two months decided to feel sorry for him instead, noting the man was in a bad mental place. "Take that one second to pull back and study them" before reacting. People in a good place don't try to destroy you.
- Reverse role model: he watched his father, mother and brother as a blueprint for how not to live. He was the youngest and learned to study people and their energy.
- Facing his father: he drove to Buffalo to face the "unsolved mystery." He researched his father and learned that the man's own father had whipped him in front of an open furnace. He said he went hoping for an apology to justify being a "loser," and instead a voice told him "it's not your dad's fault" and that he would have to make it on his own.
- "Live autopsy": examining why you are dying while still alive. He says he was living every day but really dead until he did this work.
- Face your past: "Don't ever be ashamed of anything you've done in your life. Face it, fix it, make it better." Go through the archives of your life, study it, and use it.
- Chosen suffering prepares you for unchosen suffering: do something every day that sucks.
- Trauma should not become a "Jersey barrier"; it has to be something you can maneuver through quickly.
- On the Huberman VR shark test: it didn't bother him because VR is fake and he works only in reality; if a screen scares you while you sit firmly in a chair, study why.
- Pride and a personal mission statement: have pride in yourself, write your own ethos about who you want to be, and hold yourself accountable to it each morning. "If you don't stand for something, you'll fall for everything."
- "Roger that" in its best sense means "received orders, given, expect results."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In this interview with Rob Moore, Goggins explains how he took control of his mind by confronting his past, doing what he doesn't enjoy daily, and failing on purpose. He covers the 40% rule, the cookie jar, accountability, ignoring other people's projections, and why small daily disciplines like making your bed matter.

chunks.heading: Master your mind: controlling the voice that wants comfort
chunks.text:
David describes two voices in every head. One is the comfortable voice that offers "cookies and milk at nighttime" and says "you've earned this, you deserve this." He says that voice took him to 297 pounds, a loser's life and about $1,000 a month, and ran his first 26 years.

- He wants his mind to "know who's in charge." Once you take control, you make decisions for yourself instead of your mind making them for you.
- Every day he faces the pull toward "the path of least resistance," and says you don't get better by following it, you become normal.
- On bad days he talks himself out of quitting: "So you want to be normal, you just want to be like everybody else... being fine with being mediocre?"
- Example: on arriving in London he had no running route, so he used a hotel elliptical that powers itself. After two minutes he thought "I don't want to do this," watched his mind go there, redirected it, and stayed on for two hours and 45 minutes. He adds "I'm not saying do that."
- He frames it as owning the process, not hating it: "I don't enjoy it, it's necessary." He says growth only happens in the uncomfortable zone, so he visits it every day.

chunks.heading: Face your demons: go back into the dark hole and organize it
chunks.text:
David says most people carry insecurities and issues they don't want to revisit, so they avoid them.

- His own turn came when he found the courage to "go back in there and organize that [stuff]," getting it ordered in his mind so he knew where to start.
- He compares his past to a collection of shells in a treasure chest: bad memories you hide because they remind you where you are. Once he started visiting them all, "I don't have any more shells." The flame of anger faded because there was no more fuel.
- He calls his childhood the "ultimate training ground" and says he is proud of it. Seeing the bad things that way changes how you see your past.
- Sources of pain he names: an abusive father, bullies, learning disabilities, stuttering, obesity, and repeated failure.
- His view on anger: it is powerful fuel but "can't overcome everything." He now asks what is left once the anger is gone.
- Self-knowledge process: get quiet, find the truth about who you are ("it may take months, may take years"), find your purpose, plan, then execute. He warns people love the planning phase because it is comfortable, and execution is where the real work, failure and failure again, begins.
- To do this he says to shut off technology, go dark, get away from people, and accept that being alone and even unhappy is okay.

chunks.heading: Own your weaknesses and build discipline from nothing
chunks.text:
David had "zero self-discipline" and the military did not teach it to him.

- Starting around age 16, with a fourth-grade reading level and severe learning disabilities, he forced himself to sit at a table doing reading and writing. That discipline carried over to working out.
- He argues you must "triple down" on weaknesses to become a full human being. People run toward what they are good at (the runner only runs, the reader only reads) and avoid the rest. He dove into what he was bad at.
- He shares both strengths and failings openly and says owning both is why people relate to him.
- Small disciplines matter: in the military he folded shirts and made hospital corners on his bed, and says these small habits build the mind. He says the world has lost them (rushing, no customs and courtesies).
- He warns that technology makes everything easy, so people don't use "the most powerful weapon in the world, which is your mind," and then can't rely on it when things get hard.

chunks.heading: Daily routine: win the morning, prepare the mind
chunks.text:
- David stretches for two to three hours every night. While stretching he plans the next day and the obstacles that could come up: "all things that could happen, might happen, probably will happen, and then the unknowns."
- He expects not to want to work out tomorrow and prepares his mind for it. His aim is a "mental armor" so life doesn't attack an unprepared mind.
- Winning the morning: make your bed, clean the house, eat breakfast, shower, shave, and don't hit snooze. Snooze means "you wake up already failing... behind the power curve."
- Don't grab your phone first thing, because bad news there starts your day out of control.
- Job-interview analogy: before an interview you lay out clothes, rehearse and bring your best self. After a few months you stop, and "the interview you is gone." Waking up like it's the interview keeps that standard.
- Winning the morning means you go into the world having already won something, so you can take the hits.
- Current methods beyond fitness: visualization, self-talk, deciding where he wants to be, making a plan "and I don't deviate from that plan," plenty of quiet time, and shutting out noise.

chunks.heading: The 40% rule and what suffering opens up
chunks.text:
David describes his first 100-mile race, which he ran unprepared in 19 hours and 6 minutes (101 miles). He soiled himself, urinated blood, and had 30 miles left in the worst pain of his life.

- He says he "lived 100 years" in those 19 hours: all the highs, lows, trauma, failure and success.
- At mile 70, in terrible shape with 31 miles to go, he cracked open another part of the mind. His explanation, which he ties to his "40% room": when the mind knows it is not going to quit, "it opens up... it finds more focus, more power, more drive."
- The focus is heightened to a level few examine because few are willing to go to a place of fear, suffering, pain and doubt.
- He is not addicted to it and doesn't want to live there, but knows he can go there. The experience changes how he sees people, and he sees that others can go there too.
- He admires the free solo climber (he does not name him) not for the climb but for shutting out the whole world and being willing to sacrifice everything for a few hours of total commitment. He notes he is not speaking from personal knowledge of the climber.
- He says people label such athletes "crazy" or "special" as a "get out of jail free card" so they can stay in their comfort zone, when really they just found what they want.

chunks.heading: Failure, the cookie jar, and happiness
chunks.text:
David says "failure is part of life" is a cliche when delivered by people not living it. He says he talks about failure because he is still failing today.

- You should set goals high enough that you might fail. He failed the pull-up world record attempt twice before getting it, and says everything he has done took three tries.
- Rocky analogy: watching a movie where someone keeps failing and finally wins makes you feel amazing, and he wants that feeling for himself. You can't get it without the failures. The satisfaction of success is "directly linked to the size of the failures."
- He starts to feel the success before he even gets there, and then puts that feeling in his cookie jar: "I'll come back and get you again" down the road. It can become addictive, to the point where you don't mind failing.
- His definition of happiness: overcoming yourself at all costs, reaching the point where "you don't care about being judged." You could be in a room of a million people who all hate you and not care, "not because you're angry at them" but because you know you have walked the walk and put yourself through hell.
- He says he is "the most peaceful person on the planet" because he is winning against the other voice in his head. His fun is bettering himself, though he also loves watching sports.

chunks.heading: Ignore other people's opinions, but keep an honest circle
chunks.text:
David says most people fail because they fear what others think. Other people live in your head as "puppet masters."

- Example: the first recruiter he called about becoming a Navy SEAL looked at him at 297 pounds and said he wouldn't make it. David says negative people project their own limits onto you. He notes he was only the 36th African-American to make it through in over 70 years. He also admits he avoided the military as a kid because of what friends would think.
- Don't-care means not caring how people view how you walk, talk or dress. He says when you really don't care, "you become very, very dangerous."
- But you need a small, hand-picked support staff: "if your fiancée and your kids don't believe in you... you chose the wrong support staff."
- He wants honest, truthful, accountable people in his corner who will say "you're being a turd today, you're not getting after it," not people who "kiss your ass" or pat him on the back for waking up.
- He only respects people who work hard every day, and won't take advice from people who talk but don't grind. He also warns that advice often works for the giver: a publishing agent told him a self-published book would sell around 5,000 copies, and it sold a million copies in seven months.
- His rule for his circle: if you are not trying to go somewhere, he doesn't want to hear complaints. He wants solutions, not whining.

chunks.heading: Emotion, softness, and how he built the book and brand
chunks.text:
- Emotion: you want to control your mind but you can choose when to let it out. At the VFW Americanism award, he cried for 58 seconds looking at his mom, and says that was a deliberate, earned moment. Emotional people focus on what they don't have, "pity party," and complaining produces no solution.
- Fear of public speaking: he still hates it, interviews and being on camera because of the stutter, and does it as a way of facing his fears. He prefers working alone.
- On society: he says the world has gotten "soft," with too little accountability and no acceptance that "everybody is not a winner." Toughness to him means accountability, not push-ups.
- No one is coming to save you: "the only person coming to save you is yourself."
- Business: "I'm not about money." Be authentic, have a real product (the product is himself, living what he preaches), and help people. Audiences see through fakers and the business is done. He wants to be for "the underdog."
- Book "Can't Hurt Me": he says it worked because he told the truth and was vulnerable as a "tough guy," which gave people permission. He says he is not the hero, the reader is. He was a practitioner, not a theorist, and the takeaways are basic and immediately usable ("just screw the light bulb in").
- Figures he cites: over a million copies sold in about seven months, number two behind Michelle Obama for 12 weeks, over 650,000 audiobook copies. The audiobook has him chiming in with extra stories and commentary between chapters read by a narrator.
- Best advice: his grandfather told him he wasn't going to amount to much "because of how you hang your head." He says the best thing you can do for someone is tell them the truth lovingly: "I'm watching you fail and I can't do it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins explains the philosophy behind Never Finished: discipline learned from Sergeant Jack, belief earned through work rather than hope, and the Goggins alter ego he summons when suffering peaks. He also covers taking souls, turning hate into fuel, choosing foxhole partners, and shutting off feelings to grind.

chunks.heading: Callousing the mind and the discipline of tiny tasks
chunks.text:
- David learned discipline from his grandfather, Sergeant Jack, who retired after 30-some years in the military and wore his uniform every day. Jack gave him no pity: "No one really gives a [expletive]" about what happened to him, so he could keep living or "become a statistic."
- Jack made David cut grass, rake leaves, and clean cars before and after school, and he never said "good job." Tasks were redone until they were right (one example: a thin white wall on a black tire).
- David learned to do the job right the first time rather than 20 times. The satisfaction became internal: "I don't need a pat on the back."
- His rule: "I see dirt, don't pass the dirt, clean the dirt." If a half-assed job doesn't bother you, he says, it speaks volumes about you, and you will half-ass your life.
- He wrote Never Finished from the "calloused mind" rather than from Yale, Princeton, or Harvard. He calls it a "diploma in hard knocks."

chunks.heading: The Goggins alter ego and visualization
chunks.text:
- Discipline alone wasn't enough. In pararescue training he hit the water, which he hated, and found that his ordinary mind couldn't carry him through the highest levels of suffering.
- He went into his "mental lab" and visualized a person with a "cast iron steel" mind that is "never dull" and always sharp. He wanted a version of himself that stayed and "marinated" in fear and suffering instead of running.
- He built his own training ground before Navy SEAL training, saying that anyone who arrives unprepared will quit.
- In the pool, Goggins would appear when things got hard, and "smack" David down and drag him through.
- His point: "There's no David Goggins Goggins. There's just David Goggins." Only his mindset changes. The pain stays the same.

chunks.heading: The Moab 240 porta potty moment
chunks.text:
- At about mile 200 of his second Moab 240 (240 miles, over 31,000 ft of elevation gain), he had a raw backside, broken feet, six layers of tape, and trouble breathing at altitude. He had 40 miles left.
- He lied to his pacer, Mike, about needing the bathroom, then sat in the porta potty wishing he would fall in and break a leg so he couldn't finish.
- Goggins appeared and reminded him that the course beat him in 2019, that he had trained on bad knees and visualized the course a million times, and that he was now lying to his pacer.
- He says he "knifed" David Goggins and stuck him in the porta potty, and Goggins came out. His feet and back still hurt and the pack was just as heavy. Only his approach changed: he stopped being a victim of the race.
- He ran 7-minute miles over the last stretch and dropped Mike. He used Mike's anger as fuel: "I want him to be mad at me so he can bring the best out of me."
- His advice is to keep what you want to be in the front of your mind, because you will lose it in the suffering. He says most suffering is psychological, not physical.

chunks.heading: Hope vs. belief, and who the devil is
chunks.text:
- Hope is "[expletive]" because it isn't in your hands. In SEAL training, people hoped to be pulled from the cold water.
- Belief is not the "after-school special" kind. It is harnessed through hard work and dedication, and you know what you can do because you have gone to the dark places several times.
- He kept returning to SEAL training because he believed he could make it. He knew his past failures were on him, because he wasn't executing as he should.
- He grew up watching his mother go through horrific things and was never sheltered from them. He compares it to a front-row seat at a horror movie.
- He blamed his father as the devil. When he confronted him in Buffalo, he realized "I was the true devil," the one holding himself back and looking for an escape goat. His father and mother were broken and would not save him: "You got to save yourself."
- The drive home, he says, convinced him the rest of his life would be hard because he would finally start winning.

chunks.heading: Taking souls and haters
chunks.text:
- Taking souls is rising above what a normal person would be in a situation where a normal person would be defeated, while the people around you know it. He took it from Hell Week: everyone is defeated by Wednesday, but he acted as if it were minute one, and instructors saw it.
- His boat crew thought "what one man can do, another can do" and elevated themselves, and the other crews' stunned faces became more ammunition. In his words, you "thrive in that environment" where most won't.
- People who aren't working hard can feel judged around him even though he says nothing. He compares himself to a metal detector on the beach: they run through their own "resume of life" and realize they haven't done enough.
- The hater's mixtape: he recorded everything people said about him into his phone, added beats and Eminem tracks, and played it on a loop as fuel. He studied the "mind of the weak" and concluded that you'll never meet a hater who is doing better than you. Successful people give criticism meant to help, not trash talk.
- Haters know more about him than his mother does, so he gives them "more fuel" to hate him.

chunks.heading: Having the right people in the foxhole
chunks.text:
- He started life far behind: "negative grades," having to "dig out of the grave to get to first grade." So 24 hours feels like three to five days of catching up, and he describes going to "summer school in my mind."
- The right foxhole people don't ask whether a 3:00 a.m. wake-up is smart or tell him to take a break. He needs pushing, pulling, anger, and passion, not critiquing.
- He supports everything you do, not everything you don't do. In a firefight, you don't need someone "blowing noses and wiping butt holes."
- Early in life he attracted losers because he had no "self" (self-esteem, self-awareness, self-belief, self-motivation, self-discipline). His biggest regret is not building himself fast enough, which cost him years in the "dungeon": "Everything has an expiration date."

chunks.heading: Staying disciplined with success: being "feelingless"
chunks.text:
- Success makes it harder to be Goggins: nicer beds and "silk sheets" make a 3:00 a.m. wakeup harder.
- His fix is to go back to the old school and become "feelingless" about wanting to be better. When the alarm goes off, in cold or rain, or when everyone goes home and one office light is on in a dark 15-story building, the feelings must go away.
- He says this doesn't mean turning off feelings toward family. It means turning them off in the grind.
- He didn't have talent: he shares only a birthday (February 17) with Michael Jordan and Jim Brown and can't dunk. What he could do was outwork everyone, so he gravitated to ordinary people who showed courage, character, commitment, and discipline. He calls the place where greatness begins the "blue to black line."

chunks.heading: Quitting, regret, and being a game changer
chunks.text:
- When he's considering quitting, he lists every option in the situation and then tries pairing options together. Only after exhausting every option, in his words "the accountability way beyond some accountability mirror," might he say it's not for him. He says almost no one does this, so the answer is "almost never." It takes him years, not months.
- He "front-loaded" his life: at 47 he is "100% retired," and the payoff is choices. He can say no to 99% of offers and doesn't need the money.
- Never Finished is a deeper, more philosophical book than Can't Hurt Me, which he calls a "bachelor's degree." He wrote the first one so people would know who he was. He says a third book is almost done and "puts that book to shame."
- A game changer isn't arrogant. The belief is built through hard work, so you know your value and bring "the difference to the table." You've been "training my entire life to take the big shot."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins tells how a bullied, abused, overweight kid decided the only way out was deliberate suffering, building calluses in the brain like calluses on the hand. He explains the cookie jar, the accountability mirror, flipping negative into fuel, and why greatness starts with looking inside and facing the truth about yourself.

chunks.heading: Callousing the mind through deliberate suffering
chunks.text:
- David's core idea is that the mind builds calluses the same way hands do: through repeated, deliberate exposure to pain. He calls it "callousing my mind through pain and suffering."
- At 16 he was an insecure, bullied kid in a small Indiana town, with a dad who "took our soul" and a mom working three jobs. No one helped him.
- That absence of help taught him the only person who could turn him around was himself, and the only way was "to put myself through the worst things possible a human being can ever endure."
- "To grow you must suffer." He argues most people reach a fork where left is easy and right is hard. Many take the easy route and live fine lives, but "the better life" is on the hard side, even if it costs 20 years of pain.
- He says suffering is "the true test of life," and that you cannot know who you are until it tests you.
- Example: he failed twice at the Guinness pull-up record and did 67,000 pull-ups in training before finishing 4,030.

chunks.heading: Why he runs what he hates: training for life, not races
chunks.text:
- David says he hates running, and that this is the point. "I don't want to take showers and eat either. That's life."
- He argues the person who learns to do things he hates doing finds "greatness" on the other side. He was dumb in school because he hated school.
- He defines self-discipline as "the ability to not want to do it but still do it."
- He says he is not training for a race but for life: "I'm training for the time when I get that 2 o'clock in the morning call that my mom is dead." Body, mind and spirit are trained as one so he doesn't "fall apart."
- He says he did not like jumping out of airplanes or shooting guns as a SEAL, but chose to do it to change himself. If you choose a path, you may as well be the hardest person on it.
- Attitude on the door breach: "Open the [expletive] door and go in hard." He wants people to remember that he attacked, not that he "slowly opened it and peeked in."

chunks.heading: The accountability mirror
chunks.text:
- He began shaving his head at 16 and found the mirror was the one person he couldn't lie to.
- In high school he had adopted many identities (saggy pants, pulled-up pants, different ways of talking) to fit in with groups. He calls that "pathetic."
- Every morning he reflected on lies he'd told and ways he acted to impress others, and asked "how did I attack today?"
- Tactic: if he did something he wasn't proud of, he wrote it on a sticky note and fixed it.
- Example: he wanted to sit at the cool lunch table. He wrote "[expletive] the table, sit by your [expletive] self." He did, and his table became a table people started sitting at, "because a whole bunch of people in that lunchroom felt exactly like I did."
- He says by senior year he was "a totally different David Goggins."
- Core point: "We write our own book every day, but we never read it." Read it honestly and own the flaws ("I'm a dumb [expletive]. Okay, Roger that. How do you get smarter? Educate yourself.") instead of blaming his dad, bullies or his health.

chunks.heading: The cookie jar
chunks.text:
- The cookie jar is a mental store of past failures he turned into wins: failing, going back, finally succeeding, plus things that "kicked my ass."
- In suffering, he says even the hardest people "forget how hard we really are."
- When he feels the "poor me" mentality, he takes "one second," steps out of his life, and pulls something from the jar. Example: "You were in three hell weeks and finished," including one where a man died.
- Then he puts it back and remembers who he really is: not the kid called the n-word, not the scared kid.
- He says self-talk and visualization are the two keys to his success.

chunks.heading: His first ultramarathon: breaking 30 miles into pieces
chunks.text:
- Setup: he'd never run a marathon. He wanted to raise money for the Special Operations Warrior Foundation after Marcus Luttrell's team died, and Googled the hardest races. He chose Badwater 135 (135 miles through Death Valley in summer).
- The race director said he had to qualify by running 100 miles in 24 hours. The qualifier was four days later. He was around 240-270 lb and hadn't run in over a year.
- He reached mile 70 in about 12-13 hours, then broke down: fractured shins, tearing muscles, peeing blood, unable to stand. He had been eating Ritz crackers and Mylanta, with tube socks and no water plan.
- His method: he was "driven," not "motivated" ("motivation comes and goes. When you're driven, whatever's in front of you will get destroyed"). He broke the last 30 miles into small steps: get nutrition, stand up, walk.
- At mile 81 his wife told him he wouldn't make the time. He ran the last 19 miles nonstop.
- He taped his ankles and shins with compression tape to get through. He says he first used this in his third Hell Week, taping from ankles to calves every morning for six months because of stress fractures.
- He says it became "personal": him against the race, against the kids who mocked him, against himself.
- Takeaway: "Your brain and your body once connected together can do anything."

chunks.heading: Using the dark side as fuel
chunks.text:
- He says "Goggins" is a character who can take anything. Hell Week is designed to find your flaws, and he used rage to get through.
- He wanted instructors to go home after beating him and feel worse than he did, thinking about him still suffering.
- He insists this is not Kryptonite: "I'm using it for strength. I just flip negative into positive."
- He says he is "the happiest man on the planet" and that facing what's on the other side of the door made him happy. He warns against being overtaken by it.
- In the worst moment of the race he used the negatives as motivation: "Who the hell would even get out of that chair? You did."
- He swears on purpose: he says he can't convey Hell Week by saying it "was really hard," and that tap-dancing around the truth to protect "thin skin" stops people learning from you.
- On insults: "They don't own your life." Flip it, harness it, and thicken your skin.

chunks.heading: Finding your why and living inside yourself
chunks.text:
- Advice to a lost young person: you live in an external world, so turn "yourself Inside Out." Stop listening to people calling you names; their insecurities are theirs.
- You won't find greatness in a book or in David's talk. He may give the spark, but you must be quiet, "shut the [expletive] up," search your soul and ask "why am I here on this planet?"
- First question he'd ask a kid: "Who are you at the core of your soul?" If he can't answer, "our conversation's over."
- He says greatness is not 200-mile runs or 4,000 pull-ups; it's whatever you dreamed up in your own mind. First create the vision, then ask how to get there.
- He calls most of this generation "softened," quitting the moment they're criticized, and says that makes it "easy to be great."
- Daily regimen: stretches two hours, doesn't drink or go out, oatmeal, run, weights, and keeps a very small circle of trusted people.
- Rocky I round 14 was a mental image for him, and he listened to one song on repeat for 17 hours during a pull-up record attempt.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins explains the mind's governor (the 40% rule), the accountability mirror and the dark room where you face who you are, and why you must detest mediocrity. He says drive comes from your own insecurities, knowledge comes through suffering, and callousing the mind is a daily practice, not a five-step fix.

chunks.heading: The accountability mirror: face the raw truth, then fix one thing at a time
chunks.text:
- David's accountability mirror started in his junior year of high school. He had a "1 point something GPA," missed lots of school, lied to his mom, and read at a third-grade level, which he hid by copying on everything for fear of being put in a "special" school.
- He looked in the bathroom mirror and called himself out honestly: dumb, lazy, fat, a fake "cool guy." He says he "didn't call myself out. I was just honest."
- Each day he asked: "What am I going to do today to change what I see in this mirror?"
- He argues that if you aren't "real and raw" about who you are, nothing changes. Soft language ("you're just a little big") keeps people stuck.
- Early actions were small: he stopped sitting at the cool-guy table, tucked his shirt in, and wore a "callous layer of skin" against whatever others said.
- The same honesty applied when he got fat again as an adult: "I called myself fat because I was fat."
- He says the biggest conversation of your life is the one you have with yourself: "You wake up with it, you walk around with it, you go to bed with it. Eventually, you're going to act on it."

chunks.heading: Total accountability and one-problem-at-a-time goal setting
chunks.text:
- Accountability is a daily grind, not a five-step formula. He says "It's a practice... it's a habit."
- He says the journey is a "race that you run completely alone." Social media and comparison are poison, because they show "who we want to be, not who we are."
- His mirror was covered in sticky notes: year goals, weekly goals, daily goals, hourly goals. Notes compared him to his own yesterday, never to other people ("be better than John" was not on them).
- Example: he lied constantly as a kid to be accepted. His goal became "go one day without lying." When he lied, he went back to the person and said "I lied to you."
- Progress is patient and small. Losing three or four pounds counts as a "huge accomplishment."
- He says he runs before interviews because accountability means doing what he preaches: "Are you accountable for what you're doing? ... to the T."
- He wants people to "put your life on a billboard on the busiest highway in the world" and own how messed up they used to be.

chunks.heading: The list of excuses and the "bag of..." work: accept it before you fix it
chunks.text:
- In the book he has people list everything working against them, every valid excuse and flaw. Reason: "You have to first accept it before you can fix it."
- Many people never start the journey because they live a fake life as who they want to be and haven't fixed the real problems.
- Once you fix these, you "no longer care about how people are judging you." Caring about judgment means no forward momentum.
- Method: don't stare at the whole list. Take the first item and make it a focal point, then strategize that one problem. Repeat until the list is done.
- Example, his learning disability: he can't retain information, so he built a method around his weaknesses. For his thousand-page dive manual he got the book 18 months before dive school, bought spiral notebooks from a dollar store, and wrote each page about 10 times. By test time he could recall "okay, page 71 was where I remember seeing this."
- He says to avoid trying to learn "like you" or "like anybody else." Find your own strengths and weaknesses and design around them.

chunks.heading: The 40% rule and the governor
chunks.text:
- David believes most people live at about 40% of their capability. The mind has a "governor," like a car rated for 130 mph but limited to 91 at the factory. The car wants to go, but the governor stops it.
- It is a survival mechanism that protects you from pain and suffering. When it gets uncomfortable, the mind says back off, sit down, find something comfortable.
- The mind "has the tactical advantage" over you at all times because it knows your fears, insecurities and "deep, dark lies," and steers you toward comfort.
- Practical use:
  1. Go until the mind says stop. You must get to that point first.
  2. At that moment, take control back and ask: "Let me see if I can go 45%."
  3. Keep giving yourself a little more. The mind pushes back ("we're supposed to be going right and you're going left"), and you keep controlling it.
- He says there's no tidy formula: "That's all [BS]... It's a practice... it's a habit." He thinks experts who tell you your limits are less useful than people practicing beyond them.

chunks.heading: Creating the alter ego: the dark room and "Goggins"
chunks.text:
- First, you must be unhappy with how you feel about yourself and stop running from the inner voice that says you're "wimping out." He calls the white lies we tell ourselves "okay" a trap.
- He faces the real David: a kid who stuttered and is still afraid of stammering on a show like this one.
- In the "dark room" you face who you are and then create another person to walk out. "Not like you have two different personalities. It is you. But you have to find strength."
- That person is "Goggins": someone who doesn't care about being judged, knows he's weak, knows he's afraid, and says "whatever you think about me, take it."
- He describes cracking out Goggins "like that Superman cape."
- David frames Goggins as a visualization tool, not a split personality.

chunks.heading: Turning insecurity, trauma and "no one is coming to save me" into fuel
chunks.text:
- David's background: a father who beat him, a stepdad who was murdered, a mother who couldn't coddle him, being called a racial slur at school, a learning disability, and weighing 300 lb working as a pest-control guy.
- Key realization: no one was coming to save him. When the school principal waved off the slur ("they're just ignorant"), he saw he was on his own.
- His reframe: "I had to use all this negative [stuff] that was making me weak... as the power that now fueled me... The darkness is exactly what I need."
- Others start up high with a good foundation. He started with "no legs" and had to grow them, so surpassing them felt bigger.
- On passion: "We're all looking for passion. Passion is all around you... It's your insecurities." At 300 lb he had no drive to be a Navy SEAL. He found drive in his own fear and doubt, and says "when you can find drive in your own doubt, fear, insecurities, you become very unstoppable."

chunks.heading: Detest mediocrity, don't get civilized, and keep callousing the mind
chunks.text:
- Mediocrity is "contagious." People surround themselves with others who tell them what they want to hear. David's example: someone who says "I don't feel good, take a day off, get pizza and watch the game" feels good; someone who says "get your gear on, we're running at 3:30" feels like a threat.
- Being the best of the mediocre people feels great, but it means you're still mediocre.
- Staying hungry: he doesn't sit on past accomplishments. Reaching the top of the mountain means "you got to build another one." Many people with a good resume are "one-timers."
- "Don't get civilized": comfort and retirement make people go soft (he cites retired athletes who let themselves go). He says you never retire from setting the example, because people watch you.
- Daily work: he still has to stretch for two and a half hours after the interview and hates it. "I'm constantly callousing over my victim's mentality... If you stop shooting the gun, you're not going to be a great shot." You must keep challenging the machine every day.
- He says he gains knowledge through suffering, and on the other side is "a world that very few have ever seen." At hour 19 of a 100-mile race he "found a whole another world."
- He doesn't listen to "theorists" but to people who say "I'm tired because tomorrow I got to do it again."

chunks.heading: Outwork the chart: the feeling he's chasing
chunks.text:
- His motivation isn't trophies, love or followers. "I'm in search for a feeling": true victory for himself alone, and he doesn't care if anyone knows how hard he works. He says he lives an introverted life.
- If he learns someone is grinding harder, "I'll make sure that I up my game."
- Visualization he uses: when you die, a higher power has a chart of who you were meant to be. His chart said he'd be a SEAL at 185 lb and among the smartest people. He wants to arrive and have that power say "I didn't see this," so his job is to "outwork the chart."
- Regret test: you could look back and think "I could have lived a much better life if I just would have suffered a little bit more," held back by fear and the 40%.
- At the VFW Americanism award, thanking his mother, he nearly broke down. The feeling wasn't money, fame or awards, but "I worked myself so hard that I turned a person this [messed] up into this right here... off of sheer will."
- He says everyone has a personal "equation" (like pi is 3.14) and his book, *Can't Hurt Me*, helps you solve for yours. His goal is for people to stop being ashamed of what life made them, stop judging themselves against others who "have hidden it better," and see that "life is one big head game."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins tells his story: an abusive childhood, learning disabilities, quitting Air Force pararescue, then dropping 100 pounds to survive three BUD/S hell weeks. He explains the accountability mirror, the 40% rule, the cookie jar, the first 100-mile race, and why peace comes from going to war with yourself.

chunks.heading: Childhood abuse and the origin of his fight
chunks.text:
David grew up in Buffalo, New York, with a father he calls "a devil," a violent drunk who beat him, his brother and his mother. He says his father "helped create this."

- At about seven or eight, he watched his father beat and drag his mother down the stairs by her hair. His brother hid in his room; David stayed and jumped on his father's back. His father beat him "from my neck down to my ankles like black and blue."
- Staying in the room and acting while scared became a pattern in how he handles fear.
- His mother later told him and his brother "you guys can come or you guys can stay but I'm getting the [ __ ] out of here." He went with her to Brazil, Indiana.
- At the VFW Americanism Award speech, he thanked his mother "for not picking me up when I was knocked down but teach me how to get up." He sobbed on stage for 58 seconds, then finished the speech.
- Later, as a man in his 20s, he went back to face his father. He saw a man still unchanged and reasoned that something had damaged his father and he never dealt with it, so he passed it on. David's conclusion: "I'm gonna deal with my [ __ ]," fix what he was handed, and not blame it.

chunks.heading: Trauma, learning disabilities and the accountability mirror
chunks.text:
David arrived in Indiana hiding learning disabilities, a stutter and stress that made his hair fall out in patches. He couldn't read or write well and was held back in second grade. He was also one of five or six Black kids in a school of about 1,700, with a noose and a threat drawn in his notebook. A witnessed child death and the murder of his soon-to-be stepdad in the same period left him sleeping on his floor for months. He scammed his way through school while his mother worked three jobs and never saw a report card.

- His mother's letter from the school (he'd missed about 25% of classes and was going to flunk out) was the trigger. Her only advice was that he would flunk out.
- He saw that "no one is coming to help me," not his principal, his mom or his dad. Looking in the mirror he said he was "defeated," and started writing sticky notes calling himself out.
- This became his accountability mirror: the honest conversation with yourself where the only person responsible for the change is you. He says the problem was his own mind, not anyone else.
- He later let that mirror go dirty. Spraying for cockroaches, at nearly 300 pounds, he stopped seeing himself honestly. "You can't lie to yourself," even though he could lie to everyone else.

chunks.heading: Learning by repetition: the study grind
chunks.text:
David's tutor could only be afforded for four hours a month for six months. He started at a fourth-grade reading level, and the tutor told him he'd have to write things down a thousand times to remember them. He took it literally.

- He bought spiral notebooks and wrote the same math equations over and over.
- For reading comprehension, he copied whole paragraphs repeatedly.
- He got the Navy dive manual a year ahead and wrote the book out about 14 times (Boyle's law, Charles's law, Gay-Lussac's law, Dalton's law). He can still recall a page and the act of writing it.
- His point: people think he became who he is from running. "No, I became this guy from [ __ ] study." What takes others an hour took him two days, so he put in the hours.
- He passed the ASVAB and got into the Air Force.

chunks.heading: Quitting, and why he admits it
chunks.text:
David entered Air Force pararescue and taught himself to swim, but he was negative buoyant and terrified of the water confidence training. He wanted to quit every night and slept badly. He then got a sickle cell diagnosis and was pulled from training, which was a relief because he could drop without quitting.

- When the doctor offered to put him back in with a week and some change left, he didn't want it. He lied to his commanding officer, citing sudden death risk, and took a medical out.
- He now realizes the officer knew he was quitting: "as a man, you can tell another man where the man's done." He saw that look in the eyes of the quitters when he later watched SEAL training footage.
- Why he admits it: if he only told the badass stories, he'd be a liar and a superhero fake. "I wasn't born that. I had to make myself into this [ __ ]," and he wants people to know he was a scared, depressed, insecure kid.
- Fixing the surface wasn't enough: "I'm fixing everything on the surface, I'm not going into the dungeon." People want peace without confronting their own stuff, and he says you won't find it in a yoga room: "You're gonna find peace from going to war with yourself."

chunks.heading: The turning point at 297 pounds and getting into SEAL training
chunks.text:
From about 175 pounds in 1994 to 297 pounds by 1998-99, David was out of the military, sprayed for cockroaches for around $1,000 a month and ate constantly (a milkshake from a restaurant account, a box of mini chocolate doughnuts eaten "like tic tacs," eight Pillsbury cinnamon rolls, scrambled eggs, half a pound of bacon, fruity pebbles).

- One morning he was watching a Navy SEAL "hell week" documentary in a towel with a shake. He saw guys quit and recognized his own look from pararescue.
- At graduation, a commander said "we live in a society where mediocrity is often rewarded" and that the 22 graduates detested mediocrity. David wanted to feel like those men. He was tired of lying to himself and others. He knew what he could be but was afraid the work would kill him.
- He quit his job (a roach-and-rodent dumpster night pushed him over) and started training. His first run was a quarter mile at 297, and he came home crying.
- A recruiter said he had a "lofty task": he had about three months to drop roughly 100 pounds. He dropped to about 215 on the way.
- He had to retake the ASVAB and get a 50 on mechanical comprehension. He begged the test sergeant for the score and got exactly a 50. He compares it to the stair run in The Pursuit of Happyness.
- His point: no single breakthrough fixed him. Multiple "changed" moments (the mirror, seeing his dad, the roaches) each needed follow-through. "Life is not a movie."

chunks.heading: Three hell weeks, the broken body and the duct tape
chunks.text:
David went through SEAL training (BUD/S) three times because the commander rolled back anyone who failed back to day one, week one.

- First class: stress fractures, shin splints and double pneumonia rolled him back before finishing.
- Second class: he finished hell week but broke his kneecap, and it was done ("your patella is done"). He was determined not to get rolled again, but he was.
- Third class: he got to come back with only a few months to heal a broken kneecap and stress fractures. His body was swollen by Monday of hell week. Hell week ended early on Thursday when a classmate died of pulmonary edema.
- Walk week: the instructors, angry about the death, made them stay on their feet and ruck the whole time, so there was no healing. He left home early, went to the dive cage at about 4 a.m., put on a black sock and casted his shins and ankles with duct tape as tightly as he could. The first 45 minutes were "excruciating," then his legs went numb and he could run.
- He says his stress fractures actually healed by the third phase. He's "not saying do that," but that was the choice: do it or don't become a SEAL.

chunks.heading: The 40% rule and what separates finishers
chunks.text:
David says the 40% rule is a belief he built through pain. A fat guy who quit on everything became one of the toughest men on the planet because he changed one thing: his mindset.
