- The governor analogy: some cars have a governor that caps speed at 92 mph. The factory that put it there was his own mind, and you have to take it off or you'll keep hitting the cap.
- On what separates people who finish anything hard: you have to really want to be there, and you have to have lived the suffering in your mind a million times, not just visualized the graduation. "You gotta be there in the worst and the suffering that you know over and over again."
- When suffering hits, your mind starts asking why you're doing this. If you've already pre-lived it, you have the answers ready. If you don't want it that badly, you quit.
- Inspiration in a comfortable setting (couch, fridge, a movie about badasses) disappears when the "suck factor" is real.
- His warning about "only one time": telling yourself you'll only do the hard thing once is how you set yourself up to be done. Even Special Ops guys do this. He sees athletes and others stuck in an identity built on one great accomplishment.
- He likes competition and suffering because it brings out the best in everyone. "Once you change one thing, your mindset, you can attack everything."

chunks.heading: Badwater 135: the cookie jar and 19 hours of suffering
chunks.text:
With no running base (his cardio was 20 minutes a week on an elliptical), David signed up for Badwater 135, a 135-mile race through Death Valley. The race director told him he needed a 100-mile finish in 24 hours or less, so he entered a one-mile-loop race in San Diego that Saturday.

- He ran in a hat with no shirt, fueled by Ritz crackers and no water. At mile 70 he sat down and fell apart, urinating blood, with 30 miles left.
- The cookie jar: "We forget how badass we are when we're suffering because our mind stays right there in suffering." The cookie jar is his stock of things he's accomplished and kept grinding through. He reached into it to remember.
- "I might quit, but not yet." He gave his mind space: sat, drank water, ate, stood up, and told himself he might quit later rather than panicking over 30 miles.
- He got moving again and ended up running about 20 miles at roughly a 10-15 minute mile pace, finishing 100 miles in 19 hours and 6 minutes.
- Afterward he sat in a shower, in the fetal position, passing dark brown fluid, and refused to see a doctor or take painkillers. He says the pain was proof that he'd done something unprepared, untrained and uncoached. "It was the best feeling I ever had in my life, not because of the pain, but the pain was confirmation."
- He says he learned more in those 19 hours than in three hell weeks, Ranger School and the rest, because it ran him through every emotion.

chunks.heading: Staying hungry, "taking souls" and who he's chasing
chunks.text:
David says he has to keep grinding himself "into a fine dust." What makes him him is "the dungeon," and he's only content when failing at something repeatedly until he finally completes it. He warns against settling into a place of comfort or coasting on past achievements.

- On social media and fame: he didn't set out to be a motivational figure, and he doesn't want to be pulled away from what built him. Fame can be a depression because you lose yourself in helping people. He went back to running 100 miles a week.
- His motivation: the stories in his book come from when he was living them, not from telling them. If he stops, he's no longer the person people follow.
- The pull-up record: he failed twice and finally got it (4,030 pull-ups in 17 hours), listening to one 14th-round Rocky track on a loop for 17 hours.
- "Taking souls": in the Rocky fight, he takes Apollo Creed's look when Rocky keeps getting up as the thing he wants from doubters. "I wanted a lot of people that doubted me to look like Apollo Creed did in that 14th round because I got back up repeatedly." He wants opponents to be tired from his refusal to stop.
- He says he doesn't care about winning: "I just want to go the distance."
- People who knew him at his worst, he says, try to pull him back down and don't like where they are compared with where he got to.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In the opening segment Goggins says mindset is the one change that lets you attack everything. He also explains why "I'm only doing this once" kills growth, and tells the story of his first 101-mile race. It shows the cookie jar, giving the mind space ("I might quit, but not yet") and treating pain as proof. The rest of the video is other speakers and is ignored.

chunks.heading: Embracing suffering as the way to find out who you are
chunks.text:
- David says he likes suffering "in the way that is competitive," because it brings out the absolute best in him and in everyone around him.
- He wants to be with the hardest men, suffering alongside them, and see what they are made of. His comparison: "almost like the Coliseum in Rome." The only way to find out who the baddest person is, he says, is to suffer; you can't do it by writing a paper.
- His central message: "once you change one thing, your mindset, you can attack everything."
- He used to see himself as a weak little kid and put elite people on a pedestal. Once he worked his way up there he realized "we can all compete," and he tells people not to put him on a pedestal either.
- He loves the men who get broken, say "[ __ ] you" and keep going, but says very few are willing to go there more than once.

chunks.heading: "I'm only going to do this one time" is how you cap yourself
chunks.text:
- David says many people in special ops, and in anything hard, tell themselves they will only do it once. In his words, once you say that, "you [ __ ] yourself."
- He ties this to athletes and business people who sacrifice everything once, build their identity on it, and then retell the same stories for the rest of their lives.
- David's version: he is only happy when he is grinding for something and growing. He doesn't want to talk about what he used to do.

chunks.heading: Goggins vs. David Goggins: keeping the dungeon alive
chunks.text:
- David describes two people: David Goggins, a calm, cool guy who used to be a weak kid, and "Goggin," the guy willing to tape up his legs and go after it. He says his dad created David and he created Goggin, and Goggin is who he loves.
- He says "since Can't Hurt Me came out" and he got on social media, he has been pulled into helping so many people that he lost himself. He calls this the biggest depression of his life.
- His reasoning: the book motivates people through the stories of what he did. "Once I stop living that, I'm no more." If he stops doing hard things, he is no longer the person people are being motivated by.
- He says he is now back to running 100 miles a week and back "grinding" himself, and he tells people not to get it twisted: "what makes me me is the dungeon."
- His method: "I have to be hard on myself... continue to grind myself into a fine dust." If things come easy, it isn't fun.
- He wants to fail at something repeatedly so that it haunts him, and feel he accomplished something only when he finally completes it.
- When he fails, he wants to say "Roger that," go to the dark place in his mind that people avoid because of social media and computerization, analyze what he did wrong, and work out how to get it done.

chunks.heading: Badwater 135 and the 101-mile race he wasn't prepared for
chunks.text:
- After the military, David decided to attempt Badwater 135, the 135-mile race through Death Valley that he describes as the hardest in the world. His cardio at the time was 20 minutes every Sunday on an elliptical.
- Race director Chris Kostman told him he needed a 100-mile finish in 24 hours or less to qualify. Only two qualifying races remained before the deadline. He called on a Wednesday and the next race was Saturday: a one-mile track loop in San Diego for 24 hours.
- He showed up as "a big bodybuilder looking guy," shirt off, with a blue lawn chair, and his nutrition was Rice Krispies-style crackers and a sports drink: "no water." He says he never drank water on runs and didn't know better.
- At mile 70 he sat down for the first time and everything fell apart. He was peeing blood and had 30 miles to go, in the worst shape of his life.
- He says this race, which he did without training, coaching or a crew of experts, taught him more than all three Hell Weeks, Ranger School, or his time in selection.

chunks.heading: The cookie jar and "I might quit, but not yet"
chunks.text:
- David invented the cookie jar. His explanation: "we forget how badass we are when we're suffering because our mind stays right there in the suffering."
- The cookie jar is the collection of things he has accomplished, failed at, or kept grinding through. Like a mom's cookie jar, you don't know exactly which one you'll pull out, but you reach in, grab one and go.
- At mile 70 he went back through his cookie jar.
- He told himself "I might quit, but not yet." His reasoning: with 30 miles left, your mind is spazzing, so "I'm giving my mind some space" because if you don't, it freaks out.
- Concrete steps he took: sat there for a moment, drank water, had his crew get food, and worked on simply standing up (he was dizzy and lightheaded at first). Once he could stand, he went back out.
- At mile 81 he was too slow to make the time. He says his body and mind connected and he "became a cyborg," running the last 20 miles at about a 10:15 pace. He finished 101 miles in 19 hours 6 minutes.

chunks.heading: After the race: pain as confirmation
chunks.text:
- Afterward he got in the tub in the fetal position, with the shower on him. What he passed looked like dark brown dirt rather than blood.
- His mother's friend, a doctor, told him to go to the hospital immediately. David refused: "I want to sit here and enjoy this pain."
- He says he wanted no painkillers. The pain was "confirmation," proof of what he had just done with no training, no coaching and no cheering staff. It was the worst pain of his life and the best feeling of his life.
- He says in that moment he became "the truth." He was a kid who lied and cheated, and now he was a Navy SEAL, an Army Ranger school honor man, and had done all of it.
- He says you never want an "I've arrived" mentality because you stop, but this was the moment he realized he was the truth.

chunks.heading: People who want to drag you back down
chunks.text:
- David says the people from your past, from when you were at your worst, are often mad that you're out. In his words, "they hate that they're still where they're at."
- His image: there is always "that [ __ ] in the sewer you came from that's grabbing at your ankle as you're leaving that sewer."
- He says they aren't willing to figure it out, and that "everybody has a different equation." His own equation was different from most people's, and it wasn't about being sadistic.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins explains how he turned abuse, a learning disability and 300 pounds into mental toughness by choosing the path of most resistance daily. He covers facing insecurities, building a morning armor through hard work, revisiting "scratch" to stay hungry, and refusing to settle once you arrive.

chunks.heading: The "calloused mind": rebuilding yourself by choosing the path of most resistance
chunks.text:
David says mental toughness is "not something that you sample, it's something that you live in every day." He treats the mind like a muscle that can be lost: "if you can lift 315 pounds and you stop going to the gym for a month, I guarantee you won't be able to pick the same weight up again." The knowledge he has gained disappears if he stops practicing it.

- He describes building a "callous" on the brain the way hands callous from work. Hard, repeated effort becomes part of your DNA instead of a one-time feeling.
- He distinguishes the physical standard from the mental one. At the SEAL prep program he trained recruits to be "bigger, stronger, faster," yet the same number quit at BUD/S. The standard that matters in life is a mental one: "you must know how far you've come."
- When hardship hits, people retreat to their insecurities and look for comfort, "that cookie that your mom used to give you." David says that is the moment to retrain your mind to think differently.
- He contrasts the four-lane highway with road maps, gas stations and a Cracker Barrel every ten miles against the harder route. He says the easy road is "doom" because it only buys a quick fix, while the hard road gives permanent results: "you keep a six-pack forever because you know the work that goes into it."
- He says the mind must be given no way out. Starting SEAL training broken, his only way out was death, and "when the mind gives it no way out, your body says okay, I believe you now."

chunks.heading: Morning "armor" routine and daily discomfort
chunks.text:
David says life does not hand out "get out of jail free" cards, so he builds protection before the world gets to him.

- Mornings: wakes before the day starts, does at least an hour and a half of running, then goes to the gym for pull-ups, push-ups and calisthenics. The first five hours of his day are uncomfortable on purpose.
- He does not love running: "People think I love to run. I don't. That's why I do it." He knows he will do something he dislikes every morning, and it changes how the rest of the day goes.
- Rationale: once you leave your house, "the war starts." Phone calls, social media and disappointments arrive. If you hit snooze, run late and leave a messy house, life has already beaten you before it hits you. If you have already won the morning, you face disappointments "already in victory."
- He trains at the hardest moment on purpose: after a long run, dehydrated and low on sodium, he goes straight to the gym, because "life's not going to give you a glass of water when you're thirsty."
- At night he stretches two to three hours. He has missed only two days in about five and a half years. He says it lengthens the body and opens the mind, and it is his time to recharge. He thinks about nothing.
- He says he lives around the 90th percentile, sometimes 99, because "100 is dead."

chunks.heading: The 40% rule and never "arriving"
chunks.text:
David says when you feel you have arrived, you start dying.

- After losing 106 pounds in under three months, learning to read and graduating, he realized he was "leaving so much in the tank." That is where his 40% rule came from. He says most people operate at about 40% of their potential.
- On finishing events: he used to skip the medal and ceremony and move straight on. He later learned to reflect, because he had never acknowledged how far he had come.
- His third "truth" at the end: when you finally get where you wanted to go, "be afraid." You are either getting better or getting worse. After summiting Everest, "the best thing to do is fall back down that damn mountain as fast as you can and start climbing."
- His biggest fear is getting civilized and comfortable, because "God starts to die." He wants to stay the creature "that can live in a sewer, that can eat rats, that doesn't need water."
- He insists he is not special: "There was nothing special about him. He wasn't talented, he wasn't gifted... and he made it." Labeling him as crazy or unique lets people off the hook from doing the work.

chunks.heading: Confidence, fear and self-examination
chunks.text:
- Real confidence comes from hard work and facing what scares you, not from places that feel good: "You don't gain confidence by going to the spot that makes you feel good."
- His own example: years at a kitchen table learning to read and write. He had to write everything repeatedly in spiral notebooks, and a single math problem could take ten hours. That is where his work ethic came from: "I am dumb, but I have the work ethic to catch you." He says the notebooks were empty and three months later they were full.
- He stutters severely and says his confidence comes from no longer caring if he stutters. Facing it is the point.
- He calls the process a "live autopsy": examining yourself honestly. Billionaires call him saying they are still missing something, because they did what they were good at and never examined themselves.
- Fear is no longer a word he uses. It is "my ultimate guide" to where he is supposed to be, and anything that triggers it gets conquered.
- Own your insecurities. If you're fat, call yourself fat; if you're not smart, say so. Then use that as the starting point. Stop speaking "hollow words" and staying on the surface.
- He ties maturity to this. Self-examination gives you a throttle: he rates a provocation (a level-two or level-three engagement) instead of escalating by default, unlike the old him who would pick a fight.

chunks.heading: Suffering, stress fractures and the 100-mile race
chunks.text:
- Before BUD/S he repeatedly failed and returned. For his third Hell Week he went in with stress fractures and double pneumonia. Each morning he duct-taped his feet from forefoot to mid-calf, put on two black socks and ran. The first 45 to 60 minutes were excruciating. Three months later the fractures had healed, and he says he has not had one since (he ran 7,000 miles in 2007).
- His motivation: if he could graduate starting broken among the "studs," it would change everything. "Life is one big mind game, and you're playing it with yourself. Is it true? I don't care. It got me through."
- He warns against copying this: "I'm not saying do what I did." The point is to be uncomfortable, not to injure yourself and be out for six months.
- His first 100-mile race: under-trained, four days' notice, hadn't run more than about 20 miles that year, raised money for a foundation. At mile 70, with 30 left and no one able to save him, he pulled tactics out of "the cellar of your mind." Afterward he lay in the tub, blood and brown fluid in his urine, and felt he had "cracked the code to human potential."
- Years later he got sick, had to pull out of Badwater (135 miles) at mile 50, and could not run a quarter mile. He plans to return and says he is only now in shape to go back.

chunks.heading: Delayed gratification, perspective and going back to "scratch"
chunks.text:
- He values the years, not the finish: "It's not the race, it's the 12 years." Chasing one second at the finish line leaves people angry and moving to the next goal without reflecting. Perfectionism is "the worst thing that can happen to a person."
- Perspective: he works as a wildland firefighter at 43, digging fire line (18 inches wide, three miles long, $12 an hour) beside 27-year-olds. A 21-year-old coworker looked at the mountain and his hands and decided a pair of running shoes cost too many hours of work. David keeps that story as his reminder of where he came from.
- Going back to "scratch": the further you climb, the smaller your friction gets, because you're not hungry and the fridge is full. Friction creates growth, so he visits discomfort deliberately: "Take a day trip. Don't stay there."
- Reflection: he keeps a "cookie jar" self-talk, a constant reminder of everything he's done. He says growth needs quiet, since the world is too noisy to find your purpose.
- Greatness as he defines it: being haunted, years after a career ends, by every shot you missed because your mind drifted. It is "being so aware of the time of life... and not making that same mistake again."

chunks.heading: Lessons from his father, mother and the "three truths"
chunks.text:
- Background: he describes an alcoholic father who abused him, his brother and his mother, with constant mental warfare. He grew up dyslexic, with a learning disability, a tutor and cheating, and faced racism, including graffiti on his car and a KKK presence ten minutes away in the mid-1990s. His mom worked multiple jobs and never saw a report card.
- From his mom: she never picked him up when he failed ("she never gave me that cookie"). Her stance was effectively "life sucks." He read that as a training ground and began choosing the path of most resistance.
- From his dad: "The biggest lesson he taught me was how not to be." Insecure people tear others down, and a fulfilled person only builds others up. He judges no one who bullies him because he knows where it comes from.
- His three truths:
  1. You are your own hero. Idolizing others leads to mimicry and disappointment, so hold yourself fully accountable.
  2. Never pick the easy road.
  3. When you feel you've arrived, be afraid; find the next climb.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins explains that real change means going back to the root of your childhood scars, not patching the surface. He teaches the accountability mirror (brutal honesty with yourself), the "live autopsy" of your suffering, and how the mind's protective instinct (the 40% rule) keeps you soft. He also draws on Hell Week to show how to shrink suffering into the present moment.

chunks.heading: Embracing suffering through a daily "live autopsy" of your past
chunks.text:
- David says suffering is where the answers are. "In failure and in suffering, all the answers are in there. All the answers to all the test questions, the test is your life."
- He does not mean living in suffering all day. Visit it like a workout: about 1 hour a day, with the other 23 hours outside it.
- The "live autopsy": an autopsy cracks you open after you're dead to find out why you died. David says to do it while you're alive. "Crack it open while you're alive. Don't wait until you're dead to figure out why you died."
- Steps he describes:
  - Go into the suffering and pain of your life and ask "Why did this suck for me so bad? Why am I afraid of all this stuff? Why have I shut down the whole world?"
  - Study your failures, insecurities and self-doubt for at least an hour a day.
  - Use specifics: if you're afraid to jump off an airplane, ask what makes you afraid of it and study that.
  - He went back systematically and re-met every person and every situation in his mind, one by one, and "went one-on-one with them again."
- The answers sit in the scars. "They lie within the scars. Visit them... study them. And then you'll find out more about yourself. You will then grow."
- He says he became powerful in the mind because he saw he was weak and dove into the mind instead of running from it.
- Trying to forget is where people fail. "You will continue making the same mistakes if you don't go back." Pushing the memories under the rug means there is no growth.
- He wrote his book this way. "You don't forget that stuff. You remember it. Lift the rug up, you'll find them."

chunks.heading: Go back to the root: fixing the foundation, not the surface
chunks.text:
- David says most adult problems trace to childhood. "The only way you're going to fix yourself is to go all the way back to the beginning, to your childhood, because that's where everything starts."
- His childhood: an alcoholic father who beat him, his brother and his mother about once or twice a week. Kids worked the family skating rink and bar from the time they could walk (age 4, scraping gum off the rink floor). He had a learning disability and a stutter, white splotches on his skin and patches of hair falling out from stress. At 8 his family moved to Brazil, Indiana, where he was the only Black kid. His mother worked three jobs and they lived in a $7-a-month place.
- Foundation metaphor: building on a bad foundation means "a little windstorm" can knock the house down. He looked strong but was one windstorm from breaking, and "nobody knew it."
- The turning point: he taught himself to read and write and built disciplines, yet the first real challenge pushed him back to zero. He realized he was "all surface" and needed to fix the cellar of his mind.
- He was about 24, had gone from 175 lb to almost 300 lb, and sat on his couch and realized "we got to go back," starting with his father.
- Fixing symptoms is like taking Motrin for a jacked-up knee. The swelling goes down but the knee is still damaged. "You got to fix the knee."
- He says people avoid this because they invent a version of themselves, lie about who they're not, and hide behind social media images. "That's not going to fix you."
- Doing this exposes the "scars" on the brain like scars on skin. "You have to break it open, let that blood flow... All that toxic stuff you have trapped in there has to start flowing out."

chunks.heading: The accountability mirror and brutal honesty with yourself
chunks.text:
- David calls the first step the "accountability mirror." "It starts with yourself... that person in that mirror."
- Rucksack metaphor: a military pack that civilians carry as life's baggage. His held abuse, learning disabilities, stutter, insecurity, self-doubt, immaturity, and lies told to make friends.
- No one is coming to fix it. "No one's coming back to help me... You have to realize you are on your own now." He calls it a lonely journey.
- Ownership: you have to own what others did to you. "It's yours now to fix the problems that people did to you. It makes no sense. It's not fair. I get it." Staying in a "woe is me" mentality keeps you stuck.
- The conversation must be honest, with no kind euphemisms:
  - Not "I've gained some weight" but "you're fat."
  - Not "I have a learning disability" but "I cannot read. I have a fourth-grade reading level."
  - He calls himself stupid at times, "not in a way to put myself down," but because it's honest.
  - Others: "I look like crap. I feel like crap. I'm falling behind in school. I'm lazy. My house is a mess." Call it what it is.
- He says people surround themselves with those who "tell us what we want to hear, not what we need to hear," and the inner dialogue turns into "it's okay." His line: "It's not okay anymore."
- Calling yourself out for exactly what you are, and exactly how to fix it, is where it starts. He ties this to a culture that skirts hard conversations: "We have to break the barriers within ourselves."
- Rewrite your story daily: "You have to constantly rewrite your book every day of your life." The most important conversation is the one you have with yourself, and most people's conversations "keep us sitting in that toxic environment."

chunks.heading: The 40% rule and the mind's tactical advantage
chunks.text:
- David says the mind is protective and "has the tactical advantage over you." It knows your scars, fears and insecurities and keeps you away from them.
- This is the core of the 40% rule from his book: the brain tells you to stop long before you've reached your limit.
- Examples he gives of its protective voice: don't jump out of a plane, don't go in the ocean where there are sharks, don't go back to the place where your dad beat you.
- That protection becomes a ceiling. "It protects you so much it doesn't allow growth." The mind takes the path of least resistance and wants to stay peaceful, in a "72 degree" room with a massage therapist, and away from scarring.
- You must take power over your mind or "your mind will guide you into all the soft places that your brain wants to live in."
- Watch for it mid-effort: when he revisits the past he knows his mind may let him wallow for 45 minutes, so he stays aware of the conversation he's having.
- The mind will also justify comfort: "Just sleep in today. You deserve it." David says, "Sometimes you don't deserve it... You really haven't worked hard enough."
- Aging alone doesn't create growth. People who repeat childhood patterns "strengthen a bad muscle": "I'm throwing a bigger tantrum at 43 than I did at 8."
- He agrees with Jay's monk framing that the mind is like a child and the intelligence a parent. The parent has to teach the child, not just shout at it.

chunks.heading: Hell Week: breaking suffering into the smallest moment
chunks.text:
- David did three Hell Weeks in one year (finished two), which he says no other SEAL has done. Hell Week is 130 hours of continuous training with maybe 2 hours of sleep, "designed to break a man."
- It exposes anyone who only fixed the surface, because it brings out your demons.
- Structure he describes: the first hour is loud chaos (gunfire, no time to think). In the second hour comes "surf torture" in the roughly 49-50°F Pacific, arms linked, waves crashing, now quiet. In the quiet, the mind spirals: "I have another 129 hours."
- His takeaway on the mind: it can't process 130 hours of suffering, but it can process right now. "The brain can't handle hours and hours and hours of suffering. But it can handle right now, I'm in the Pacific Ocean and it's very cold." Break big painful things "down to the smallest molecule."
- Tactics he lists:
  - Stay in the exact moment. He does not think even an hour ahead, such as about eating.
  - Think about the people beside you. As a boat crew leader he checked on his five teammates ("How was John? How was Andy?"), and his mind stopped caring how cold he was. "If you don't think about yourself, there's no pain."
  - Get a different vantage point: "Get on top of that mountain top in your mind and look down on what you're doing... that world is beautiful." Spiritually get out of the suck and be amazed at how far you've come.
- He describes himself as a practitioner, not a theorist: "A theorist is a person who reads a book, doesn't do it. A practitioner... put yourself in hell repeatedly and study how you process it."
- He says he studied this on himself through Hell Week, Ranger School and other schools, and the tools came from watching how the mind speeds up in hell.

chunks.heading: Recovery, burnout and the "hard stop"
chunks.text:
- David warns that the "think about others, not yourself" trick can't be used every day. It's like a lever that gets rusty and has to be oiled. "There has to be a recovery process for your mind, your body, your soul, your spirit."
- He says he lost about 5 years to overdoing it and is "just now back to crushing it." He talks about this in the last chapter of his book. He credits meditation, stretching, eating right and sleeping right over 5 years.
- Pushing hard is good, but "to push as hard as you can, you have to be mindful of the machine that's pushing. It is going to end up dying."
- Warning signs he uses:
  - You can't hear yourself think; your mind is "so amped up."
  - Every day is a schedule and you have no time for yourself.
  - You start saying "I don't have time for this anymore" and neglect your fiancee, your disciplines, reading, learning, workouts, diet, sleep.
- His rule: when he drifts too far from those self-disciplines, "it's a hard stop," because those disciplines are what made him who he is.
- He listens for an internal "unrelenting voice" (the dedication in his book is "to the unrelenting voice in my head that will never allow me to stop"). He calls it right-or-wrong voice, whatever name you give it. The more you ignore it, the quieter it gets until you hear only yourself. It often points toward the uncomfortable choice, like getting up instead of going back to sleep.
- His fiancee conversation is part of the check: he tells her "Hey, I'm doing too much."
- He balances pushing: "constantly grinding myself into a fine powder, but doing it in a smart way... There's a happy medium of grinding."

chunks.heading: No special people: stripping the superhuman label
chunks.text:
- David says labels like "superhuman" or "1%er" give people "a get-out-of-jail-free card." He wrote his book raw so readers could see where he came from.
- "There are no special people. There are special minds, and the mind can be created on your own."
- The mind forgets quickly: by chapter 9 or 10 of his book, readers forget chapters 1-3 of the hell he came from. He says the same happens when he speaks: "By the time I leave... you forgot it already. The mind's already tricking you." So keep reminding yourself of chapters 1, 2 and 3.
- Daily mantra: "I used to believe I was the weakest man that God ever created. So now I believe that I'm the hardest human being that God ever made. I don't care if it's true or not, it's the most important conversation to me."
- Other points he makes:
  - Don't forget your roots as success grows. Return to the quiet place of the "dirty mirror" in the $7-a-month place where he grew.
  - Be wary of motivational speakers who don't live it: "Are you actually doing what you say you're doing?"
  - Let people evolve. Don't pull someone back to who they were. If someone's growth makes you feel bad, "fix yourself" and "change your own life." He cites Good Will Hunting: the friend who wants you to leave is the kind to keep.
  - His advice on advice: he never received any, so the best advice came from himself: study yourself, including the good, and grow. The biggest thing that can hurt him is himself, by letting his mind build a false reality.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins tells an entrepreneur crowd that greatness is only 1% away and most people are weak, so maximizing minimal potential wins. In Q&A he covers building belief, studying fear, the 450,000 seconds of Hell Week, facing his old 300-lb self, taping yourself on bad days, and choosing a foxhole that keeps you in the fight.

chunks.heading: Winning by default: why most people are weak
chunks.text:
- David argues that "it's easy to be great nowadays cuz most [people] are weak."
- He says there is a big difference between 99% and 100%. He always thought he was giving 100% and wasn't, so he was only 1% away from the money, the life, and everything he dreamed of. That 1% is what people "sleep on": the morning they say "not today, maybe tomorrow."
- His tactic is to think about all the weak people taking a day off while he keeps working, and he says he "will come up real fast."
- During COVID, others used closed gyms and cancelled events as excuses. He says the people who kept training on a trail or at a playground pull-up bar "marched light years ahead."
- He calls this "maximizing minimal potential." If the average person has 10% potential and wastes nine of it, then using your 2% fully beats them. He says he was born with nothing but realized most people are lazy.
- Leaders who stop get passed. People rest, you don't, and you pass them.
- He says people look at him and see potential. He sees accomplishments, because he used every bit of what he had.

chunks.heading: Unbalanced life, front-loading, and having no finish line
chunks.text:
- David says he decided about 23 years ago, when he called himself a "born loser," to go all the way in.
- He argues that to be in the top 1% you have to throw balance "in the wind." He tells his family: "I'll be home, but not today."
- He calls this front-loading. You grind early and bring your family fully on board at 40, 50, or 60, once you have made the money.
- He says an unbalanced mind does everything at a level others can't fathom. People see you grinding while they sit at a mediocre level, and you rise slowly.
- He is 47, a smoke jumper out of British Columbia, and says he has plenty of money but "ain't [enough]." He says there is "zero finish line."
- He compares himself to his bulldog, who will eat until she's dead: "I leave no scraps on the table for anyone to pick up."
- He says he wants to be "the hardest [person] ever lived." He doesn't know if he is, but putting it on the table keeps him closer to it.
- Whatever you think about, he says, "will become exactly who you are." Greatness starts in your head, and most people never put it on their list.

chunks.heading: Building belief, the unseen work, and the dog
chunks.text:
- David says he failed the first 24 years of his life because he hadn't developed belief. He insists this is not "Sesame Street" talk like "believe in yourself."
- He builds belief through hours, days, and decades in the grind, and says he gained his "by going into the damn dungeon and staying there." He runs 100-mile and 200-mile races, breaks pull-up records, and jumps at 47 because he has to build belief at that level given the darkness he came from.
- When he fails, he goes back to the "belief jar" and pulls out the belief he built. It tells him he failed because he "didn't figure it out yet," not because he can't.
- He calls his daily work "the unseen work." Nobody knows what he actually does. People see a one-minute snippet, and on Instagram he dumbs things down because the truth would get him called a liar.
- He built an "insanely high pain tolerance" and a "dog" inside him, and says the pain, the lonely nights, and being unbalanced make you dangerous once you have the right people with you.
- He says belief can't come from a book or a motivational speaker.
- He says nothing in his journey needs changing: "I had to do all that to continue on with the belief I have to have to move forward every day." Everybody has a dungeon, some deeper than others.

chunks.heading: The one-second decision and trying one more time
chunks.text:
- David's core advice is: "Try one more time."
- He failed SEAL training the first time, and also Ranger school, Delta selection, and a pull-up record, and got "really [messed] up" in smoke jumping training. He says look at where he is now.
- Hell Week is 130 hours, but he says it's the 450,000 seconds that make people fail. You can get 449,000 right and lose by one second.
- For a 100-mile run, he says not to think about 24 hours. Do the seconds. That is how much focus it takes in whatever you do.
- His own first 100-mile attempt was at about 300 pounds with no training, which he calls the dumbest thing he ever did.
- His advice to someone moving from 100 to 200 miles is to get scientific about recovery: "It's not so much the distance, it's the recovery." He did eight 100-mile runs in eight consecutive weekends.
- He gave a pull-up injury story: a doctor gave him a morphine shot in the palm of his hand and he kept going, and "that shot hurt like hell. For a second."
- On limits, he says they are all relative.

chunks.heading: Facing the old self, anxiety vs fear, and the tape recorder
chunks.text:
- David says the 300-pound pest-control version of him never goes away. When he runs, the figure chasing him isn't a skinny shadow, it's that 300-pound man. He now turns around and faces it each morning and says, "I know you ain't going nowhere, but you have to control every decision you make in your life."
- He says it's not a permanent solution. The demons always want to break you back down, and that's why he keeps building belief.
- He wants to go to bed "net positive": "I'm in the black, not in the red." He may wake up negative, but before bed he puts the demon to bed.
- On fear, he says he studies it. Fear lasts a second (looking out of a plane at 15,000 ft), while anxiety, the day or two before a jump, lasts a long time. He studied parachutes, how they're packed, how they open, and the malfunction procedures, until he was "a genius at the [thing] I was afraid of" and the fear drifted away.
- His tape recorder trick for bad mornings: record how you feel when you wake up, then play it back and ask if it would get a friend off the couch, or whether his girl would sleep with him tonight. He says to listen to how weak and pathetic it sounds, then get up.
- Everything you say to yourself should energize you "to the core of your soul." The weak voice takes the path of least resistance, so smack it down fast. He says "even me" doesn't want to work that hard.
- He also described a "lab for my brain" where he does a "live autopsy," constantly dissecting why he stops short of the finish line. He says everyone has something holding them back, and you have to face your own shadow or hit the prison wall.
- He described the accountability mirror as a tool he used.

chunks.heading: The foxhole, empathy, and leading versus managing
chunks.text:
- David's "foxhole mentality" says that when you go to war every day because you want to be great, you can't have losers from high school or college in your foxhole.
- He wants people who, when he's suffering, ask if he wants a banana, a drink, or coffee while he studies late, not people who give weak sympathy. When he's hungry they feed him, when he's tired they keep him up, and when he says he can't, they help him find a way and "never give me a way out."
- He gave the example of a woman who wanted to be a doctor and got stuck in anatomy. Her parents said she didn't need it, and now in her 40s she regrets it. A good foxhole partner would have said "I'll get you a tutor."
- He says there is a place for empathy "but not when you're trying to be great." He says "have about this much" of it, and staying in empathy too long ruins your team.
- A manager makes sure you clock in every day, and a leader knows you and doesn't baby you so you can become the best you can be. Teach your team thick skin, not empathy, because "it's not here to hurt you. It's here to help you."
- On joining a team as a lone wolf, he says he used to storm in with "let's go, and if you can't, [forget] you," and they resisted. Now he takes time to learn each person's ins and outs and what motivates them, then sprinkles seeds until "trees" grow in their brain. Each individual gets a different leader from you, and they follow because they trust you.
- He says the person who joins the lone dancer is the real hero, because they make it okay for everyone else. He says the first follower started his movement, not him.
- He says as the first to do something, you're setting the example and if you stop leading, no one follows. Leading "never ends."

chunks.heading: Discipline needs direction, goals, and a mission statement
chunks.text:
- Asked by a 26-year-old who didn't know what he wanted and lacked discipline, David said you can't have discipline when you don't know where to put it. You must first have plans, goals, destinies, and a journey, and then the other questions fall into place.
- You won't find it at conventions or in a book. At around that age he sat down and thought about who he wanted to be and what that looks like.
- He told the man to go home, shut off the phone, the TV, and the world, and "tune into you."
- He tells people to write a mission statement covering where they see themselves in 1, 2, 3, 4, and 10 years. Don't live just to wake up, kiss the wife and kids, and punch the clock. On days you don't know why you're doing it, open it up. He says SEALs and Rangers have creeds for this reason.
- He says figure yourself out before attaching to a family, since if you're not your best self you give your family a half-assed person.
- When he runs out of goals, he goes through his "Rolodex" of what he hasn't done, and especially what he hasn't done at an elite level, and checks them off. He calls it a witch hunt for whatever makes you tick. Once you start "living civilized," he says, it's over, so keep the savage as long as you can.
- He says the goal is to be able to "operate without purpose at the highest level possible."
- Asked what goes on his headstone, he said a person "who just tried one more [time], every time." He says he's scraping dust because he front-loaded and lives with a paranoia that he's missing something.

chunks.heading: Overcoming setbacks and anchoring against burnout
chunks.text:
- David's turning point was spraying for cockroaches at around 300 lb in a restaurant at 1 am, when he realized "this is the rest of my life" and didn't want to die a born loser. A recruiter told him he had a few months to lose 106 lb for the Navy SEALs. He says he "put everything on black, put everything on David Goggins."
- After a bad surgery on his leg he gave himself 24 hours to feel sorry for himself, then went back to the grind. He had a 3-month plan to find the best doctor. They sawed and reset his tibia and put in a plate, which normally takes 18 months to recover from. At 8 months he ran 100 miles, and he was jumping out of planes at 9 months.
- Asked what he'd do if he couldn't run, he said he would be the best cyclist on the planet.
- Before SEAL training's third Hell Week, which his instructor said was his last attempt, he went in with stress fractures and shin splints. He says that when you believe it's really your last shot, "you'll find inhumane [stuff]" in you and make it.
- For burnout, he uses words as mental anchor points, like climbing anchors that limit your fall to 10 to 12 feet. He says hope is not an anchor point and he doesn't live off hope. His rule: "One day you'll sleep, but not today."
- On a breakup and a divorce, he said to suck it up, stop the feelings, and move on if the person doesn't want you. He said you attract the same level you're at, and he was married three times while "in the dungeon." When he became who he wanted to be, he found a partner who also wanted to up her game.
- On marriage, he says he was honest with his wife for three years: "I'm a savage, this won't be fun, support me differently." Everything in the house has to be aligned and "you can't tightrope" it.
- For parents and moms who can't throw balance away, he says to use every free hour, such as when the kids and husband are asleep, and that if you don't, "you did not want it bad enough." He also says to give kids chores and responsibility to build mental calluses, since "if you don't teach them that, no one else is."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins recounts going from 300 lbs to Navy SEAL through three Hell Weeks, then running 101 miles with no training. He explains how he calmed his mind, refused to give himself a way out, used the cookie jar, and built discipline through daily routine and refusing to get comfortable.

chunks.heading: From addiction to ambition: how David lost and regained 106 pounds to chase SEAL training
chunks.text:
- David joined the Air Force at 19, about 175 pounds, to become a pararescueman. He was uncomfortable in the water, hated it, and treated a sickle cell finding as "a way out." He quit training.
- After quitting he went from about 175 to about 300 pounds. He says he "started finding things that made me very comfortable," and that was the start of the downhill slide.
- He served about four years as an Air Force Tactical Air Control Party (TACP) airman, then got out and sprayed for cockroaches at about 297 pounds.
- A Discovery Channel show on Hell Week brought back how badly the water had messed with him mentally. His takeaway: when you run from something and don't handle it, it keeps bothering you. That pushed him to try to become a SEAL at 297 pounds.
- Recruiters hung up on him for about two weeks. He kept calling until he reached a Navy reserve recruiter, Steven Sal Joe, who "gave me a shot." "I was just looking for a shot."
- The requirement: lose 106 pounds in under three months.

chunks.heading: The weight-loss method: math, obsession and high-rep training
chunks.text:
- David did the math: about 3,500 calories per pound, so stagnation was not an option. His mind "became very obsessed."
- He barely ate. He had a banana in the morning and otherwise "pretty much don't eat."
- At 300 pounds his legs hurt too much to run, so for the first roughly 50 days he rode a bike (even while watching TV) and spent a lot of time in the pool.
- He trained all day with extreme volume: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 reps on one exercise. Example: about 10 lb on each side of a 45 lb bar, repped around 100 times, for a few sets. He credits this routine with keeping his skin tight, with little excess skin.
- He called the recruiter at odd hours (like 11 at night) to report workouts, and the recruiter at first did not believe he would do it.
- The cost: he went from 297 to 191 pounds and developed stress fractures before BUD/S even started, so he arrived "already broken."

chunks.heading: Failure, three Hell Weeks, and learning to stay in the fight
chunks.text:
- First BUD/S attempt: stress fractures and double pneumonia, rolled back to day one, week one. Second attempt: he made it through Hell Week, but a fractured patella (suffered before Hell Week) kept him from keeping up, and he was rolled back again. He graduated on his third attempt, completing two Hell Weeks. He graduated August 10, 2001, in class 235, which lost a man.
- His old pattern: when something got hard in pararescue training, "the best thing to do... was just quit." He found an excuse, or lied (he blamed sickle cell).
- What changed in BUD/S: "the harder it was, the more it was challenged in my mind," so he had to find different ways to stay in the fight, and that made him tougher.
- He says he is happy he went through three Hell Weeks: "I actually needed it." Self-examination is something every person has to do, and Hell Week was one of the best places to do it.
- Earning the Trident did not satisfy him: "All I wanted was more... it started in Hell Week and it's still going now at 43."

chunks.heading: The first ultramarathon: Badwater, 101 miles on zero training
chunks.text:
- Motivation: after Operation Red Wings, David knew the fallen men (Danny Dietz, Michael Murphy and Axelson through BUD/S or training) and was at military freefall school with Morgan Luttrell, Marcus Luttrell's twin brother. He had to give Morgan the news. The story moved him to raise money for the Special Operations Warrior Foundation, which covers 100% of college tuition for children of fallen special operators.
- At the time he was about 250 pounds and a powerlifter. He found the Badwater 135 (Death Valley, summer) and called the race director on a Wednesday.
- Qualification required running 100 miles in 24 hours or less. His resume (Ranger School, Air Force training, three Hell Weeks) did not matter, only that. A qualifying race was that Saturday, three days later. He had run about 20 miles in the whole year.
- Result: 101 miles in 19 hours 6 minutes on a one-mile track with "zero training."
- He says this is where he realized he was "scratching the surface of the human mind."

chunks.heading: Controlling your mind at mile 70: the step-by-step process
chunks.text:
At mile 70 he was peeing blood, dizzy and lightheaded, in the worst shape of his life, past his previous furthest run of 26 miles. His process:

1. **Calm the emotion first.** "Emotion controls us, we cannot let emotion control us." He says his worst decisions came when his mind said "let's get the hell out of here, we're done, this sucks."
2. **Don't give yourself a way out right now, but let the mind believe it has a little control.** Tell yourself: "I might quit, but not now." He calls it giving your mind "a little cookie." If the mind knows you won't quit, it spazzes more.
3. **Fix the physical problem.** Dizzy meant hydration, salt, potassium and more nutrition. Then he stood up.
4. **Shrink the task.** He did not think about "30 more miles." He asked whether he could walk a mile, then two. At mile 81 his crew said he would not make the time, so he asked, "Let's see if we could run a little bit now" and ran the next 19 miles.
5. **Use the cookie jar.** After calming down you need something that fuels you and gets you out of the chair. He reflects on times just as hard as this, including his rough childhood (detailed in his book "Can't Hurt Me").

His broader insight: when we hit pain and suffering, "the wall gets bigger and bigger" and the mind says to quit. Finding ways around that wall is the work, and it took years of practice.

chunks.heading: Why he keeps doing it: leading by example and daily discipline
chunks.text:
- Early on, the motivation was overcoming himself: he saw himself as weak.
- Now, at 43, he says it is about being a leader and setting the example. "I can't talk it and not live it." He will not talk about what he used to do; he has to still be that guy.
- Routine:
  - Runs every morning, no day off since December 2016. He wants to "win the battle in the morning."
  - Stretches two to three hours daily; missed about two days in roughly five and a half to six years.
  - Weights about four days a week ("you can't just be a runner").
- He calls this the "monotony" of his life and says it is how he builds discipline, while noting he is not telling everyone to copy it.

chunks.heading: Staying hard after the SEALs: "day one, week one" every day
chunks.text:
- David served 21 years, retired, and says he misses nothing about the Navy because he left it all out there. Even on deployment, if the call came at 1 a.m., he was in the gym at 1:05 a.m. He also underwent two heart surgeries.
- He lived every day "like it was day one, week one of BUD/S," even after graduating and while recruiting and instructing, because even "the biggest baddest person in the world" gets comfortable once they finish something hard.
- Lessons he took from the Navy:
  - Teamwork is big, but you must be a good individual first and "triple down on your weaknesses." Your teammate may not be there, so be a jack of all trades.
  - Accountability: go back to boot camp in your mind. People are happy to leave boot camp and SEAL training, but those are what make you good. Over time people get comfortable, sag, and lose the "militant discipline."
  - Values and discipline are a muscle: "you stop going to the gym, stop running, you get weak." Keep up the discipline of whatever school or training shaped you.

chunks.heading: Advice on joining the military
chunks.text:
- He thinks everyone should do at least two years in the military.
- Start with mindset, since everything in the military is about mindset. Most people only work on themselves "at a surface level." He urges going deep into your demons and what actually drives you.
- Handle your own problems before you enlist, because the military will expose them and push you to question why you're there. The military then "fine-tunes who you are."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins tells his story of abuse, a learning disability, and quitting pararescue, then deciding at 297 lbs to become a Navy SEAL. He explains the 40% rule (the brain puts a governor on you), callousing the mind through practice, facing your weaknesses in the mirror, and why motivation fades but being driven lasts.

chunks.heading: Childhood trauma, learning disability, and the starting point
chunks.text:
- David was born into an abusive home in Buffalo, New York. His alcoholic father beat him and his mother. At about eight years old, after one of the worst beatings, his mother got him out, and they moved to Brazil, Indiana.
- He grew up in a small town near a KKK hub, one of about five black families, and was bullied and had a racial slur spray-painted on his car through high school.
- He had a severe learning disability and cheated through school. By his junior year he read at a third-grade level, and his mother never saw a report card.
- He says the toxic stress left him unable to retain information, and he stuttered badly as a kid.
- To pass the ASVAB (he scored a 20 on his first try) he had six months, four hours a month of tutoring at $15 an hour, and hand-copied entire manuals into spiral notebooks. Something that takes others an hour took him six or seven days.
- His point: he started from a "horrible foundation" and nobody was coming to fix it.

chunks.heading: The turning point: 297 pounds and "indestructible mental toolbox"
chunks.text:
- After leaving Air Force para-rescue training (he lied about the medical situation to get out, and says he didn't tell anyone for years), he ballooned from 175 to 297 pounds.
- He sprayed for cockroaches at Ecolab for about $1,000 a month, working 11pm to 7am, then ate a large chocolate milkshake and a box of mini donuts on the drive home. "I was depressed and food felt good."
- He saw a TV show on SEAL training. The commanding officer said: "We live in a world where mediocrity is often rewarded. These men did test mediocrity."
- He realized no one was coming to help: "Everything was on me and solely on me." He decided to start building an "indestructible mental toolbox" and announced he would become a Navy SEAL.
- Recruiters hung up when he said 297 pounds. The one who agreed to see him told him he had three months to lose 106 pounds. He lost the weight in about two and a half months.
- He quit his job the same day after a cockroach-spraying incident, and says his best workouts come "when you're least motivated."
- "I had to stop thinking normal. I can no longer be a common man walking around doing common things."
- "Being a badass hurts real bad and that's why I didn't want to do it."

chunks.heading: The 40% rule and the governor on the brain
chunks.text:
- At the 24-hour race in San Diego (needed to qualify for the Badwater 135), he sat down at mile 70, urinating blood and with his blood pressure collapsing. His ex-wife, a nurse, told him he was turning white.
- He called it the worst pain of his life, and he has done 21 years in the military and 60 ultra races.
- His tactic was to shrink the problem to the smallest possible step: "Let's not quit yet. I'm going to quit, but not yet."
  - Get nutrition, then quit after the peanut butter and jelly sandwich, "but not yet."
  - See if he can stand. Walk to the car. Get back to the chair.
- He then did 30 more miles and finished 101 miles in 19 hours.
- The governor analogy: a car factory-limited to 91 mph could do 130. We put a governor on our brain, and at that limit the body starts asking questions ("this sucks, let's stop").
- "If you can't answer the questions your brain is asking you, you quit." If you have a quick answer to "why the hell am I out here," the brain shuts up.
- He says the brain has a tactical advantage because it knows your insecurities, lies and fears. Even on stage, his mind still tells him to run off, as it did in a sixth-grade play where he stuttered. He counters by recalling his "resume," what he's been through.

chunks.heading: Callousing the mind and being a practitioner
chunks.text:
- He says he is not a theorist: "I studied it by being a practitioner. I put my mind in hell."
- The analogy: he did 67,000 pull-ups in nine months, which calloused his hands against the bar. He used the same idea to "callous over" his victim mentality.
- Examples of what he endured while training: three Hell Weeks in one year (130 hours of continuous training, about two hours of sleep, restarting from day one after ruptured hernia, a broken kneecap, and 16 stress fractures).
- For the stress fractures he taped his ankles to his shins with duct tape and ran on his hip flexors for the first 45 minutes, until the pain subsided.
- He later ran 7,000 miles in 2007 to raise $2 million for the Special Operations Warrior Foundation, on a heart with a dime-sized hole (an atrial septal defect), which he says explains why doctors couldn't understand how he did it.
- On mental toughness books: "It's all crap" because they're cookie cutter. "We're all different equations." You must figure out your own equation first.
- His book is called Can't Hurt Me. "Life isn't fair... it's a trial ground, a testing ground built to make us harder." His line: "Nothing should be able to hurt you. If you believe that it starts to become true."

chunks.heading: The mirror, accountability, and facing weaknesses
chunks.text:
- His turning point came from the daily bathroom mirror, where "you can't lie to yourself." He shaved his head young and lied constantly to be accepted.
- That inner voice "started gnawing at me so horribly" that he had to go down into the "dungeon," the sewer where his mind used to be, and talk to that guy.
- His goal: not money or fame but to impress "the guy in the mirror," and to die proud.
- He says the first step is "face yourself and be accountable for what you're not, so then you can be what you want to be."
- As a SEAL instructor he realized he was only building "bigger, stronger, faster quitters" because he changed external things and not the internal.
- He doesn't "triple down on strengths," he triples down on weaknesses. He hated the water, and facing it is what made him a SEAL and gave him a story. Fears are doors to another world that people keep shut.

chunks.heading: Motivation, noise, and the other side of suffering
chunks.text:
- "Motivation is crap." It peaks when bills are paid and everything is good. The test is when everything falls apart and you still get it in. You need to be driven or obsessed.
- The world is too noisy (phones, computers) to hear yourself. "You have to be alone in a very dark place in your mind" to work out what you want and your purpose.
- The "box" analogy: the 40% rule keeps us in a comfortable box with highways, restrooms and gas stations. Outside it, "God gives you a shovel" and you dig your own path.
- "On the other end of suffering is a life that many people don't know even exist." He is now 185 pounds.
- Climbing analogy: he stopped fearing walls once he learned how to climb, with the ropes, shoes, chalk and harness.
- Inspiration: he believes he was put here for a reason, and that his suffering was to "unlock the code of human potential" and share it.

chunks.heading: Leaving nothing on the table (the heaven chart)
chunks.text:
- What haunts him is the 24-year-old at 300 pounds who could have died as a 300 to 400 pound man in a minimum-wage job, "never knowing that I was this guy."
- His visualization: God has a chart showing what you were supposed to be. His would show 185 pounds, a 205-mile run, a pull-up record, and motivating people. He wants to have written "more" on it with a marker, to impress God.
- His book test: imagine giving your book to a stranger as you die. If it wouldn't change their life forever, rewrite it.
- He turned down a $300,000 publishing offer for Can't Hurt Me, saying he wouldn't sell his story, and self-published.

chunks.heading: Leadership, authenticity, and being your own hero
chunks.text:
- Leadership: "being very uncomfortable all the time." You hold yourself to a near-untouchable standard, may lose friends, and may have an unbalanced life.
  - Example: if the team trains at 5am, the leader runs to work at 3:30 to remove every excuse.
  - "To wake up every day miserable and say 'God, I don't want to do this anymore,' that's when you know you're a leader." He calls it Groundhog Day.
- Authenticity: be able to put all your bad, not the good, on a billboard and walk around saying "this is me, but I'm fixing it." Not caring what others think.
- Role models: he respects the "uncommon among uncommon," people who stand alone, hold morals, and go right when everyone goes left. He dislikes yes-men.
- "We are our own hero." People let you down because they're human, so hold yourself accountable, look up to yourself, and don't try to mimic anyone: "Don't be them, be you."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins tells how a cracked, abusive childhood and a victim mentality led him to build a calloused mind through relentless work. He explains the cookie jar, the "what if" mentality, tripling down on weaknesses, and why self-talk only works when backed by real work.

chunks.heading: Callousing the mind: from victim mentality to a calloused mind
chunks.text:
- David grew up with what he calls a "cracked foundation": an alcoholic, abusive father (abuse of him and his mother), a move to a small town in Indiana with about five Black families where he was regularly called racial slurs, a stutter, social anxiety, a learning disability, and cheating through school.
- With no one to show him the way, he says he had to "mend that cracked foundation alone."
- He had a victim mentality: his dad, society and his mom had messed up his life, or he was "dealt a bad hand."
- He argues mental toughness was not enough. He developed what he calls a "calloused mind," and used it to get over the victim mentality by outworking his faults.
- His method for building it: do something every day that sucks, and "triple down on your weaknesses, not your strengths."
- He says the skill is not natural talent: "I'm not the best person to run... I'm not the smartest." What he learned was to outwork everybody around him, and that work ethic is how he became known as the hardest man on the planet.

chunks.heading: Setting your own standard and rejecting mediocrity
chunks.text:
- David argues society rewards mediocrity as if it were a standard. Beating ten mediocre people in a race or at work still leaves you mediocre.
- Most people reset their standards to whoever came before them. He set his own standard and "reinvented the wheel" for himself instead of following the crowd.
- He doesn't try to be Michael Jordan or Tiger Woods: "I'm trying to be like David Goggins." In his view, true growth is finding yourself and conquering yourself.
- He stopped comparing himself to others and compares himself only to himself. "Don't worry about what everybody else is doing, worry about what you're doing."
- He also says everyone who judges you has problems of their own.
- On social media he posts his bad side and what he has to work on, because everyone has a side they show and a side they are not working on.
- He thinks more people relate to struggle than success: most people are underdogs, and very few are the one-percenters (CEOs, the best golfer). Everyone loves the Rocky story, but you have to work your ass off to create one.

chunks.heading: Staying uncomfortable: friction and sharpening the sword
chunks.text:
- David says he doesn't live a glamorous life, though he says it's not because he is broke or lacks the means.
- His analogy: a boxer with a four million dollar house goes to the mountains for about two months before a big fight, living on a cot or the ground, to put his mentality in a ready state. David says he lives that way all the time.
- He is "always sharpening my sword": "my refrigerator is never full, I've never arrived," and every time he gets close to the top of the mountain he falls back down on purpose.
- He believes starting from scratch is true growth, and that "there has to be friction in your life for you to be able to move forward."
- On excuses: people triple down on their strengths (runners only run, readers only read), so when life presents a challenge they aren't good at, they quit. His alternative is to say "I'm not good at it, I'm going to be great at it."
- He says you can't fix anything in life until you fix yourself, and that most people avoid looking inside because what they find is ugly: lies, secrets and insecurities. Once you rip those layers away, the other end is who you truly are and you have no more excuses.

chunks.heading: The Rocky visualization (round 14)
chunks.text:
- With little in the way of role models, David became obsessed with people at the bottom, and with Rocky in particular. At 43 he still returns to round 14 of Rocky I, which he first watched around age 10 to 12.
- The scene: a no-name boxer against the best in the world, Apollo Creed. Rocky is knocked down roughly thirty times, his coach Mickey tells him to stay down, and Apollo turns his back and raises his arms thinking he is done. Rocky pulls himself up on the ropes with nothing left.
- What David took from it: Apollo's look of "who the hell are you?" He wanted every obstacle and every doubter to look at him like that, and as he describes Rocky: "I don't care if I win... I just want to keep coming after you."
- He visualized that scene for years. For him it became a reality he had to live: "I had to become that guy who can run on broken legs going through hell week."

chunks.heading: The cookie jar
chunks.text:
- David describes the cookie jar as a mental reminder to use when your mind and body say you're done. He says even the hardest person on earth forgets how badass they are when times get hard.
- Mid-race, with the mind spazzing out, take one second and go into the jar, which holds everything you have overcome, suffered through and fought through.
- His example: running 205 miles non-stop. At mile 100, after more than 24 hours, his body is broken with 100-plus miles still to go.
- His version of the self-talk: "you went through two hell weeks, you went through Ranger School... I've overcome a hell of a lot more than this."
- The purpose is to remind yourself you have the strength to persevere, not be mediocre and not settle for what is in front of you.

chunks.heading: Defying the odds: the "what if" mentality
chunks.text:
- David was about 297 to 300 pounds when he set the goal of becoming a Navy SEAL. Nearly every recruiter told him there was no way, saying he had to lose so much weight so fast.
- One recruiter told him there were only 35 African Americans to ever become a Navy SEAL in over 70 years. David got into his truck and asked himself, "but what if I could?", and decided to try to be the 36th.
- He says people who can't imagine something reflect that doubt onto you like a mirror. He takes that mirror and discards it, and uses all their negativity as fuel.
- He says he could have stayed a 300-pound man spraying for cockroaches at 24, and that most people walk the earth as a fraction of what they are capable of.
- What drives him now is being his best, which he calls a never-ending journey, and "finding more of myself." He says he is the most driven person in the world because he realized he was leaving so much on the table.
- He holds that you open up another world once you peel the crust away and see who you really are. He thinks people who never try to get to the other side of what is in front of them are the crazy ones.

chunks.heading: Self-talk only works with the work behind it
chunks.text:
- David's book Can't Hurt Me (out December 4 per the interview) is a self-help memoir. He says it is not a five-step program but is about getting to the root of the problem, which is yourself: "Master your own mind and everything else is taken care of."
- His mantra: "can't hurt me." He used it during SEAL training, Ranger school, fights and tests, and on a bully or a failure. He says it becomes true only if you put in the work to develop a calloused mind.
- During long events (for example mile 75 of 135 through Death Valley) he tells himself he is the hardest man God ever created. He says he doesn't care whether it's literally true, he believes it.
- His caveat: "Self-talk without the work is just lies." When he talks to himself in a bad spot, he is also recalling the 3 a.m. wake-ups, the 15 miles a day for 75 days with no days off, and the roughly three hours of training a day, so the self-talk is real.
- His analogy: telling yourself you'll pass a test you haven't studied for won't get you the result.

chunks.heading: Practitioner versus theorist
chunks.text:
- A theorist, in his picture, is the old man in a library reading about how the brain is supposed to work. Theorists put invisible bars and barriers on what humans can achieve.
- A practitioner goes out and does the work: "A practitioner dives into suffering and as he's suffering he's writing the book."
- His example: Hell Week is roughly 130 hours, and at hours 48 to 72 your mind is a mess. It is easy to write about it in a 72-degree library, but a practitioner writes it in 50-degree water when everyone is quitting.
- His advice is not to read about it but to put yourself in the environment and listen to how you talk to yourself in the worst situations. That is how you build real self-talk, real visualization and real tools for hard times.
- His closing line: "You have to be willing to suffer to get to the other side. The other side of suffering is a whole other world that people have no idea even exists."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Live DC talk where Goggins tells the Badwater qualifier story behind the 40% rule (the mind's governor), the cockroach-to-SEAL turning point, and the difference between ego and confidence. He stresses that the new self is not permanent: you decide who you want to be and earn it daily with unseen work.

chunks.heading: The war inside: who you are versus who you want to be
chunks.text:
David says the real fight is internal. At 24 he was overweight, bullied, abused and hiding it, and he points to that guy as the baseline he fights every day.

- Change is not permanent. "I wake up every day" and go through the steps again to become Goggins.
- He asked himself who he wanted to be: "a guy that can endure... whenever he doesn't, he does."
- He painted that picture in his mind, then looked in the mirror each day until he felt like that man. The standard was how he felt, not how he looked.
- His advice: get off social media, stop measuring yourself against others, spend time alone figuring out what you want to be, and be that person.
- People change clothes, houses and partners but "most of us just don't change how we think." He decided to grow the day he chose to go after Navy SEAL training, and calls it a painful decision because the effort felt unbearable to comprehend.
- Dreams are not enough. "Dream big. But don't make dreams your master." The change happens when you put work into the dream. He had no mentor; if you fail, he says, own it and don't blame anyone.

chunks.heading: The 40% rule and the mental governor
chunks.text:
David built the 40% rule out of his first 100-mile race.

- The governor is like the speed limiter on old cars: at a set speed the car stops giving more. Our brains do the same, except "we are the factory" and we install the limiters ourselves.
- The more pain, suffering and toxic experience in a life, the more it pushes you back to that governor.
- Release it by getting to a place that is uncomfortable, where the brain says "we're good," and then holding on a little longer.
- Proof: two weeks after the 100-miler he could barely walk, tried a quarter-mile run two days before a marathon and couldn't. When the gun went off he "took off like a bat out of hell" and ran a 3:08 marathon that qualified him for Boston.
- He says this capacity is in everyone, and many people in the audience think they can't because of limits they put on themselves. He asks readers of *Can't Hurt Me* to remember the first 125 pages: the kid with no self-esteem who lied, cheated and made excuses.

chunks.heading: The 101-mile race: pressure release valve and small stages
chunks.text:
David describes his first ultra, a 24-hour track race on a one-mile loop he entered cold to qualify for Badwater 135.

- Setup: after Navy SEAL training (three Hell Weeks) he was a heavy lifter whose cardio was 20 minutes a week on an elliptical. He had days to prepare, ran with no nutrition or electrolyte plan, and ate Ritz crackers and Myoplex. He was about 225-230 lbs.
- At mile 70 he sat in a lawn chair, dizzy, with low blood pressure and unable to stand, and was soiling himself and urinating blood. He calls his ego "busted."
- Pressure release valve: when the mind is full of clutter, he told himself "I'm going to quit." That relieved the tension, but in the back of his mind he knew he wasn't leaving. He says he is not recommending this, but it worked for him.
- Then he took stages: clean up first, eat real food (peanut butter and jelly, Rice Krispies treats, water, Gatorade), then "one mile," then "just one more."
- At mile 81 his wife told him he would miss the cutoff if he kept walking. He ran the final 19 miles averaging a 10-minute mile and finished 101 miles in 19 hours and 6 minutes.

chunks.heading: Rebuilding from 297 pounds: the SEAL decision
chunks.text:
David explains how he went from the cockroach-spraying job to Navy SEAL training.

- After the Air Force, he went from 175 to 297 pounds in about 18 months, depressed. He hid his weight from his best friend, who thought he had become a pararescueman. Living a lie, he says, haunts you if you have any self-esteem.
- His routine: a 42 oz chocolate milkshake, mini chocolate donuts, and at his mom's house eight cinnamon rolls, half a dozen eggs, almost a pound of bacon and cereal.
- A TV show on SEAL training (class 224) ended with the officer saying "We live in a society where mediocrity is often rewarded. These 18 men appear to test mediocrity." David: "I'm not even mediocre."
- Recruiters laughed at him. Recruiter Steven Saljo weighed him at 6'1" and told him he had about 3 months to lose 106 pounds. David said "Watch" and gave up the milkshake.
- The turning point came while spraying a restaurant: a dropped brownie, a wand pulled by his own arm, and roaches falling from the ceiling tiles. He walked out to the truck and quit.
- He recalls losing the weight (106 pounds in about two and a half months) as the hardest thing he ever did: no one cooked for him, he made $1,000 a month and worked relentlessly.

chunks.heading: Ego versus confidence
chunks.text:
- David likes confidence, not ego. "Ego almost got me killed several times."
- Confidence means "I know what I know." It comes only from putting in time, work and effort, especially the unseen work.
- Ego is what you have when you haven't done the work. He says he was a Navy SEAL who had never run 100 miles and believed he could, so the race buried that ego.
- On self-esteem: telling kids "you're great" does nothing "if you don't put the time in and the work in."

chunks.heading: Leadership: "Who's going to carry the boats?"
chunks.text:
David tells the origin story during Hell Week with a boat crew that included Chris Kyle.

- Boat crews have six men. The heaviest part is the front, so the strongest go there and the weakest at the back. David always took the front: "When you lead, you must carry the heaviest load of the group."
- One teammate kept "ducking the boat" so the weight rested on others' necks. David talked to him repeatedly, then asked whether he really wanted to be there. The man said no.
- David's lesson on teamwork: you talk to someone until you realize there is no more talking to do; they just don't want to be there.
- When David moved him to the front spot, the man tried to turn around and ask him to come back up. David refused: "I've been up there for 72 hours."
- When the man quit, the crew's energy left with him. David returned to the front and yelled, "When you leave, who's gonna carry the boats and the logs?" The crew got back under the log.
- A leader must look for the moment to re-energize people when things fall apart. "Be that guy that wants to stay when it's minus zero and snowing."
- He says the energy of his stage persona is the same one that comes out of him in the pain cave, and criticizes speakers who don't live what they preach.

chunks.heading: Advice for athletes: a war mindset
chunks.text:
David's answer to a track athlete who wanted to raise her teammates' intensity:

- Frame it as a mindset: go to the limit "where someone's life ends and yours begins." In a race, you hear a rival's breath fade as you pull away, and that is taking their soul.
- Motivation is not enough. Give the team facts. Make them work so hard that they step to the line knowing nobody else has done what they did today.
- Look left and right at the start and think: "You don't even know who you're dealing with."
- Extra work must be visible to teammates for them to follow.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Goggins argues that comfort kills growth and mental toughness is built only by repeatedly facing what you don't want to face. He illustrates it with his first 100-mile race, where he broke the pain into chunks, calmed his mind, and refused the path of least resistance.

chunks.heading: Callousing the Mind by Doing What You Avoid
chunks.text:
David argues that comfort is the reason people stop growing. He says "we live in a world that we want to be as comfortable as we can," and that when the smallest thing gets difficult, people "cower and run away" because their whole life is built on the path of least resistance.

- He ties this to his own life: he became 297 lb because that was comfortable. Running, dieting and facing things he didn't want to face were what felt uncomfortable.
